PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

But voting for - or against - this high-stakes ballot measure in November is not as simple as voting for - or against - Prop 40.
That's because Props 41 and 42, which never mention billionaires but are backed by some of the state's wealthiest residents, are also on the ballot and have provisions that conflict with Prop 40.
(Props 41 and 42 do not conflict with each other.)
Under the California Constitution, if two conflicting measures on the same ballot both pass with more than 50% of the vote, the one that gets the most "yes" votes prevails.

Newsom’s poison-pill problem
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones)
10/26/2026 09:00 AM EDT
California Gov. Gavin Newsom attends a rally with members of the state's Democratic Party, organized labor, and other advocates in San Francisco, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. | Heather Diehl/AP
DOUBLE TROUBLE — If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to Gavin Newsom . But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible. One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%. And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
Newsom, a likely presidential contender, already has taken considerable political heat (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/11/billionaire-tax-gavin-newsom-01070600) for his opposition to Prop 40, which he says would devastate California’s finances (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/newsom-unloads-on-california-wealth-tax-proposal-00723732) by pushing wealthy taxpayers out of the state. Newsom’s poison-pill problem
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones)
10/26/2026 09:00 AM EDT
California Gov. Gavin Newsom attends a rally with members of the state's Democratic Party, organized labor, and other advocates in San Francisco, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. | Heather Diehl/AP
DOUBLE TROUBLE — If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to Gavin Newsom . But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible. One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%. And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
Newsom, a likely presidential contender, already has taken considerable political heat (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/11/billionaire-tax-gavin-newsom-01070600) for his opposition to Prop 40, which he says would devastate California’s finances (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/newsom-unloads-on-california-wealth-tax-proposal-00723732) by pushing wealthy taxpayers out of the state. And if Prop 42 ends up blocking the tax over the will of the voters, it would only give more fuel to critics accusing the governor of carrying the billionaires’ water.
Rep. Ro Khanna has hammered that point as he and Newsom circle each other ahead of a potential presidential matchup. Khanna has leaned into the wealth tax as a way to both bolster his progressive bona fides and differentiate himself from Newsom, and he has excoriated Newsom for backing Prop 42.
“If a majority of Californians vote yes on Prop 40, that’s a mandate to make billionaires pay their fair share,” Khanna said in a statement to Playbook. “Overturning that through the billionaire-funded loophole that Governor Newsom is championing would be a betrayal of the voters who fought for this. The Democratic Party has to decide whether it stands with working people or with the donor class. I know which side I’m on.”
Advertisements for Prop 42 do not directly link the proposal to the billionaires tax. Proponents are instead emphasizing the other main component of the measure: a prohibition on new taxes on financial assets such as stocks and retirement accounts.
“Californians should never have to worry that politicians will come after the retirement savings they spent a lifetime earning. Yet five proposals in recent years show that the threat is real,” said Brian Marvel , president of the law enforcement union Peace Officer Resource Association of California, which has endorsed the initiative. “Prop 40 is just the latest example of this emerging threat. …Whatever happens with Prop 40, Prop 42 gives Californians the long-term protection they deserve.”
But to Prop 40 backers, Prop 42 is inextricable from the efforts to quash the billionaire tax. The fact that deep-pocketed opponents funding the anti-Prop 40 campaign have spent nearly $40 million on advertising for a second measure that could kill the tax illustrates the lengths they are willing to go — and the resources they have at hand. (The same group behind Prop 42 also qualified a second measure, Proposition 41, which has been largely abandoned.)
Newsom did not elaborate on his reasons for backing Prop 42 when he rolled out his endorsements this month, but people close to him say his position is an extension of his long-standing opposition to a state-level wealth tax.
Some members of Newsom’s orbit acknowledge the potential of both measures passing could be politically explosive, but said it’s not a particularly pressing concern, mainly because they are increasingly certain the billionaires tax will fail. Private polling from three separate polling firms — FM3, Public Opinion Strategies and Binder Research — have consistently shown the measure hovering in the high 30s or low 40s, well short of the majority it would need to pass.
That is a notable divergence from public polls, which have regularly shown Prop 40 with a slight edge, usually with a plurality that falls short of 50%. That is a precarious place for a ballot measure (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) in the closing weeks of an election, but a more optimistic view than the opponents’ internals.
If the measure does pass, the political blast radius could be vast. It would be a jolt to the Democratic political establishment — including gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and powerful interest groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood — which led its imprimatur to the ‘no’ side. It would put billionaires like Brin and other ‘no on 40’ funders on notice that populist fury at growing wealth inequality is strong enough to overcome a deluge of political spending.
And for Newsom, it would put him on a losing side of the issue, even as he has called for raising taxes on billionaires on a national level (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/26/newsom-calls-for-national-billionaires-tax-00977751) and has struck other populist notes, including backing public equity stakes in the profits generated by artificial intelligence companies.
SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez blasted Newsom for abetting what she called a cynical scheme to disenfranchise millions of voters, calling Prop 42 a “misleading and dangerous threat to Californians.”
“Governor Newsom is in lockstep with his billionaire-backers,” Jimenez said in a statement. “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors: he’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask 200 billionaires to finally pay their fair share.”

The Thompson campaign responded with a letter from seven of those former staffers who take issue with Adams-Falconer’s assertion and are demanding the Jones campaign remove the image from the ad.

Newsom’s poison-pill problem
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones)
10/26/2026 09:00 AM EDT
California Gov. Gavin Newsom attends a rally with members of the state's Democratic Party, organized labor, and other advocates in San Francisco, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. | Heather Diehl/AP
DOUBLE TROUBLE — If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to Gavin Newsom . But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible. One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%. And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
Newsom, a likely presidential contender, already has taken considerable political heat (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/11/billionaire-tax-gavin-newsom-01070600) for his opposition to Prop 40, which he says would devastate California’s finances (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/newsom-unloads-on-california-wealth-tax-proposal-00723732) by pushing wealthy taxpayers out of the state. And if Prop 42 ends up blocking the tax over the will of the voters, it would only give more fuel to critics accusing the governor of carrying the billionaires’ water.
Rep. Ro Khanna has hammered that point as he and Newsom circle each other ahead of a potential presidential matchup. Khanna has leaned into the wealth tax as a way to both bolster his progressive bona fides and differentiate himself from Newsom, and he has excoriated Newsom for backing Prop 42.
“If a majority of Californians vote yes on Prop 40, that’s a mandate to make billionaires pay their fair share,” Khanna said in a statement to Playbook. “Overturning that through the billionaire-funded loophole that Governor Newsom is championing would be a betrayal of the voters who fought for this. The Democratic Party has to decide whether it stands with working people or with the donor class. I know which side I’m on.”
Advertisements for Prop 42 do not directly link the proposal to the billionaires tax. Proponents are instead emphasizing the other main component of the measure: a prohibition on new taxes on financial assets such as stocks and retirement accounts.
“Californians should never have to worry that politicians will come after the retirement savings they spent a lifetime earning. Yet five proposals in recent years show that the threat is real,” said Brian Marvel , president of the law enforcement union Peace Officer Resource Association of California, which has endorsed the initiative. “Prop 40 is just the latest example of this emerging threat. …Whatever happens with Prop 40, Prop 42 gives Californians the long-term protection they deserve.”
But to Prop 40 backers, Prop 42 is inextricable from the efforts to quash the billionaire tax. The fact that deep-pocketed opponents funding the anti-Prop 40 campaign have spent nearly $40 million on advertising for a second measure that could kill the tax illustrates the lengths they are willing to go — and the resources they have at hand. (The same group behind Prop 42 also qualified a second measure, Proposition 41, which has been largely abandoned.)
Newsom did not elaborate on his reasons for backing Prop 42 when he rolled out his endorsements this month, but people close to him say his position is an extension of his long-standing opposition to a state-level wealth tax.
Some members of Newsom’s orbit acknowledge the potential of both measures passing could be politically explosive, but said it’s not a particularly pressing concern, mainly because they are increasingly certain the billionaires tax will fail. Private polling from three separate polling firms — FM3, Public Opinion Strategies and Binder Research — have consistently shown the measure hovering in the high 30s or low 40s, well short of the majority it would need to pass.
That is a notable divergence from public polls, which have regularly shown Prop 40 with a slight edge, usually with a plurality that falls short of 50%. That is a precarious place for a ballot measure (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) in the closing weeks of an election, but a more optimistic view than the opponents’ internals.
If the measure does pass, the political blast radius could be vast. It would be a jolt to the Democratic political establishment — including gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and powerful interest groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood — which led its imprimatur to the ‘no’ side. It would put billionaires like Brin and other ‘no on 40’ funders on notice that populist fury at growing wealth inequality is strong enough to overcome a deluge of political spending.
And for Newsom, it would put him on a losing side of the issue, even as he has called for raising taxes on billionaires on a national level (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/26/newsom-calls-for-national-billionaires-tax-00977751) and has struck other populist notes, including backing public equity stakes in the profits generated by artificial intelligence companies.
SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez blasted Newsom for abetting what she called a cynical scheme to disenfranchise millions of voters, calling Prop 42 a “misleading and dangerous threat to Californians.”
“Governor Newsom is in lockstep with his billionaire-backers,” Jimenez said in a statement. “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors: he’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask 200 billionaires to finally pay their fair share.”

WHERE’S GAVIN? Nothing official announced.
WHERE’S KAMALA? In Milwaukee, campaigning with Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley and appearing at a town hall with NAACP President Derrick Johnson .
CAMPAIGN YEAR
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (left), and Randy Villegas, Democratic candidate for congress in California's 22nd District, wave at the end of a campaign rally on Oct. 23, 2026, in Bakersfield, California. | Jae C. Hong/AP
CLASS FOCUS — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made no mention of Prop 40 or the measures meant to undercut it as she rallied for progressive House candidate Randy Villegas in Bakersfield on Friday.
She didn’t spend much time discussing her and Villegas’ similar ideological profiles, either. Instead, the potential presidential candidate, who has not endorsed the wealth tax, emphasized their working class origins, saying Villegas’ family’s story, immigrating from Mexico and starting an auto body shop, was the “American dream at work, where we start from nothing and we make something of ourselves.”
She compared his upbringing, working in the shop before becoming a political science professor, to hers, helping her mom clean houses growing up.
RELATED: “ AOC can draw a crowd. The midterms will test whether her politics can win before 2028 (https://apnews.com/article/aoc-ocasiocortez-midterms-progressive-president-2028-2d75354a3a5685efc65ff5ab9b7401a6) ” by the AP’s Joy Cappelletti
Villegas echoed the class-based appeals that have become foundational to their wing of the Democratic Party, while railing against Speaker Mike Johnson ’s recent visit to the Central Valley to campaign alongside his opponent, Rep. David Valadao . He urged attendees to tell their family members to vote, before joking: “Call your ex. Make sure they get their ballot in, but only if they’re going to vote for us, right?”
RELATED: AOC stops by In-N-Out burger during California campaign trip (https://nypost.com/2026/10/24/us-news/aoc-stops-by-in-n-out-burger-during-california-campaign-trip/) by the California Post’s Geoff Earle
Rep. Mike Thompson speaks with reporters after a news conference on Sept. 30, 2025, in Washington. | Mariam Zuhaib/AP
STAFF SPAT — The intra-party fight between Rep. Mike Thompson and challenger Eric Jones has spilled into a dispute between Thompson’s former staffers. The dust-up began when Jones released an ad (https://x.com/andrewsolender/status/2114083961836089529?s=46) featuring Thompson’s former communications director, T.J. Adams-Falconer , accusing the Democratic representative of being in office too long and part of a “corrupt political system.”
“Mike Thompson told me directly he plans to die in office,” Adams-Falconer says, before saying he’ll be voting for Jones. The ad shows a photo of Adams-Falconer standing next to the congressmember, along with other staff members.
The Thompson campaign responded with a letter from seven of those former staffers who take issue with Adams-Falconer’s assertion and are demanding the Jones campaign remove the image from the ad.
“Collectively, we have served Congressman Thompson for over thirty years, and none of us have ever heard the Congressman say anything of the kind,” the letter reads. “What we have heard him say is precisely the opposite — that he does NOT intend to die in office.”
Meanwhile, the Thompson campaign is hitting Jones for pouring more of his personal wealth into the contest. Jones loaned his campaign roughly $5 million this month, according to FEC filings, bringing his total investment in the race to nearly $15 million.
“Voters will not be deceived by a San Francisco venture capitalist air dropping into our communities to buy a seat in Congress,” Thomas Dowling , Thompson’s campaign manager, said in a statement.
ON THE HILL
House Financial Services Committee Ranking Member Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) walks to a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, on June 9, 2026. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WATERED DOWN — The center-left Majority Democrats, which represents younger Democratic officials, deleted a post criticizing Rep. Maxine Waters , 88, and the Capitol Hill “gerontocracy,” Jasper Goodman reports (https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/10/23/congress/democratic-group-walks-back-gerontocracy-swipe-against-maxine-waters-01134350). The deletion came after one of the group’s members, Rep. Ritchie Torres , pushed back against the post that appeared to take aim at Waters’ campaign to continue as the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee.
STARLINK SLOWDOWN — A trio of House Democrats representing Silicon Valley demanded that the White House investigate reports that SpaceX limited its military-grade version of Starlink satellite services to Ukrainians on the battlefield, writes Owen Dahlkamp (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/23/starshield-slowdown-probe-democrats-01133720).
In a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles , Reps. Sam Liccardo , Jimmy Panetta and Khanna asked for a briefing within two weeks outlining who decided to restrict Starshield speeds, how they were implemented and if any contractual obligations were violated. The lawmakers also asked for details of whether similar vulnerabilities exist elsewhere.
The Wall Street Journal has reported (https://www.wsj.com/world/ukraine-starlink-elon-musk-trump-dbc49193) that Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of Starlink and that he spoke with President Donald Trump and other senior administration officials before the limits were imposed.
DOWN THE BALLOT
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: DOWNSTREAM IMPACT — A candidate in the typically sleepy race for Board of Equalization is trying to ride the wave of spending in battleground congressional districts as he seeks to flip the state’s only Republican-held constitutional office and seat on the panel. The campaign for Fresno City Councilmember Nelson Esparza , in a memo set for distribution to prospective donors, party leaders and labor unions, argued that the 1st BOE district’s overlap with the competitive districts of Valadao and Rep. Adam Gray , and its slight Democratic voter registration edge, make it prime for a flip. Esparza is facing term-limited state Sen. Shannon Grove for the open seat, which is currently held by Republican Ted Gaines .
OLYMPIC GAMES
CARRYING THE FLAME — San Jose is pushing to be a torch city during the 2028 Olympics, vying for a chance to have the Olympic flame cross through the city on its way to Los Angeles. The torch will move through all 50 states for the first time during the LA games, according to Mayor Matt Mahan ’s office, with its final path announced next year. The city’s council is set to consider the proposal on Nov. 3.
CALIFORNIA CURRENTS
PACK YOUR BAGS — Climate-related disasters have forced thousands of Californians out of their homes in the last few years. Some have moved to new communities, while others have left the state, and experts are warning that this is merely the beginning. Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Summary
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West

What your vote means
Yes
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
No
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
More on Proposition 42
For background on Proposition 42, an analysis by the legislative analyst, endorsements for and against the measure, and more...
Read the California Voter Information Guide (http://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/).
Arguments
Pro
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
Con
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
The Yes on 42 side has a large money edge, roughly 5.6 to 1 once you count the Yes on 40 committee's spending on Prop 40 against it. I'm now weighing historical base rates for California initiatives that poll under 50% late, since those usually fail, though that pattern is mostly for measures where "Yes" means change, and here it may not apply the same way.

I'm weighing whether heavy spending on a Yes campaign actually secures a win, since Prop 22 with $200M won while Prop 27 with $170M lost badly. Here the big money is behind Yes, so the usual pattern of heavy No campaigns winning doesn't carry over neatly.

Prediction markets have dropped sharply on Prop 42 as of November 2, with Kalshi and Polymarket both falling. I'm wondering whether late polls or early vote data caused the drop, so I'll look for news from November 1 to 3. I also want to check how the market on Prop 42 compares with the one on Prop 40.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.

Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no.
