As I’ve written, the idea faces healthy skepticism (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/07/mamdani-nithya-raman-housing-socialism-abundance-00817314). One centrist critic calls Left-YIMBYism “capitalism for developers, communism for landlords.” But its supporters believe its potential success could end the left’s housing wars and lead to an enduring, renter-centered political coalition.
Tyler Katzenberger: Will tech’s spending spree in state legislative races pay off? A North Bay Assembly contest between fellow Democrats Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward offers a test: Grow California, funded by crypto executives Chris Larsen and Tim Draper , has cumulatively spent more than $1 million backing Lucan and opposing Elward, labor’s favored candidate. A Lucan win would help validate the industry’s strategy of swaying state politics by spending big in Dem-on-Dem races, while an Elward victory would be a triumph for labor leaders who increasingly find themselves at war with tech interests.
The race also has high stakes for Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas , who ruffled feathers among the Legislature’s Black and Progressive caucuses (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/11/rivas-assembly-senate-endorsements-01144382) by endorsing Lucan, who is seen as the more moderate candidate, over Elward, a Black woman and self-identified progressive.
Lindsey Holden: Proposition 39, California’s voter ID ballot measure, once looked like it might have a real shot. Polling earlier this year suggested the concept was broadly popular (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/05/04/california-democrats-voter-id-00905425), and Democrats were slow to mount an opposition campaign (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656). But in the months since the primary, voting rights groups, labor, legislative leaders, Gov. Gavin Newsom and his likely successor, Xavier Becerra , all lined up against it (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/24/california-dems-ramp-up-anti-voter-id-fight-01011990), relentlessly yoking the measure to Trump.
The messaging seems to have paid off. The measure is trailing in polls (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-voter-id-measure-falling-short-in-new-poll-01127047), and the president’s ongoing efforts to exert control over California’s elections (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/10/15/california-noncitizen-voting-lawsuit-01121542) likely isn’t helping Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio create the bipartisan coalition he would have needed to make it law.

All Haley breaks loose
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white)
11/02/2026 09:00 AM EST
Voting stickers | David Swanson/AFP via Getty Images
DRIVING THE DAY — Gavin Newsom redoubled his support for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , after his rival in the primary, Haley Stevens , made a shock endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday morning.
But Newsom’s response — a post on X (https://x.com/GavinNewsom/status/2116963882321547624?a=a81hx_WxO-5-yTzeKvQ&s=20) affirming his support for El-Sayed without mentioning Stevens — was notably less lacerating than other Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , who said Stevens committed a “despicable betrayal.”
Appearing on the YouTube show 2Way (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ppJFvSvw5yY), Newsom was asked by conservative co-host Larry O’Connor whether Democrats were being hypocritical after years of urging Republicans to choose country over party and break with Trump.
“I don’t know enough about what ultimately led her to make that decision outside of what she said in that video. And she certainly has the right to do that, and I don’t condemn her on that basis. I don’t agree with her, and made that point clear,” Newsom said.
That was not sufficient for frequent Newsom antagonist Rep. Ro Khanna , who posted on X (https://x.com/RoKhanna/status/2117066889553650073?a=eHCTLwwsrEUVOUhEhso&s=20) linking the lack of condemnation to Newsom’s opposition to the billionaires tax, adding Newsom’s “Big Tent is just standing for nothing.”
Meanwhile, Kamala Harris recorded robo-calls supporting El-Sayed in Michigan. She did not make a public comment about Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers.
BEYOND THE TOPLINE — The California governor’s race sits at the top of the ticket, but Xavier Becerra vs. Steve Hilton isn’t where the drama is. That’s down the ballot.
These are the races that POLITICO California reporters will be refreshing on election night. Among them are a ballot measure that tests just how much voters want to stick it to billionaires, the Democratic incumbents who may be swept out by demands for generational change, and a pair of contests in Los Angeles that could establish democratic socialist dominance in the nation’s second largest city.
Here are our picks of the top races to watch.
Melanie Mason: Yes, the Los Angeles mayor’s race is the marquee contest in the city (more on that below). But don’t sleep on the little-watched city attorney’s race, where Marissa Roy , a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, appears poised to defeat (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-28/marissa-roys-lead-grows-over-john-mckinney-in-la-city-attorney-race) John McKinney , a centrist Democrat running on a law-and-order platform. While Nithya Raman ’s relationship with DSA has been fraught, Roy’s race has been a top priority for the group. If both Raman and Roy win their races, it would mean candidates from the insurgent left will occupy all three citywide offices (controller Kenneth Mejia , also a progressive, already won reelection outright in June with a commanding 63% of the vote). The prospect of a total progressive takeover in the country’s second-largest city would be a major flex for the ascendant DSA — and would make Los Angeles the leading laboratory of progressive governance.
Jeremy B. White: I’ll cheat a bit and say I’m curious to see the fate of three Democratic incumbents facing viable, well-funded Democratic challenges for safe seats: Rep. Doris Matsui in Sacramento, Rep. Mike Thompson in northern California and Rep. Jimmy Gomez in Los Angeles. So much of the focus has deservedly been on whether Democrats win the reconfigured Prop 50 districts to secure a majority. But at a time of generational turnover and roiling anti-establishment discontent — plus a dose of scandal (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/19/jimmy-gomez-house-ethics-sexual-misconduct-staffer-01041651), in Gomez’s case — blue seats could flip, too. Democrats will likely reclaim the House. But it’s less clear what they’d do with power — and that’s largely because of the kind of internal divisions on display in these races.
Blake Jones: Moderate Democrat Adam Gray and progressive populist Randy Villegas , who are both running in competitive districts in the Central Valley, could tell us a lot (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/09/how-to-win-the-central-valley-01113264) about how the Democratic coalition is moving. Each should perform better than Democrats did in their respective regions in 2024, given the atmosphere we’re in. But if Gray or Villegas does so by a noticeably larger margin, that would be a signal that their brand of politics is faring better in the Valley, and likely, among their districts’ Latino voter majorities. If they perform similarly — or if Gray only gets a slight edge from his incumbency advantage — that would be a sign that voters are simply moving away from Republicans and not toward a specific kind of Democratic message.
Will McCarthy: It has been 15 years since Occupy Wall Street brought the issue of wealth inequality to the center of political discourse in the United States. Billionaires and their bottomless resources had a growing influence over the political system, and the concept of the 1% and the 99% became a familiar part of the American political lexicon.
But years later, through three presidential campaigns and countless Bernie Sanders speeches, voters until now have never had the chance to weigh in on the issue in such a direct way as Proposition 40, a one-time tax on California’s billionaires. The issue pits a fractured coalition against an opponent with endless resources, and the polling suggests the measure is running behind. But will voters, who routinely express a dour view of billionaires (https://www.dataforprogress.org/blog/2026/8/13/voters-think-billionaires-earned-their-wealth-through-exploitation-not-hard-work), vote to pass the measure simply to stick it to the man?
Daniel Miller: Los Angeles’ mayoral race is a strange brew of grievance and policy. Incumbent Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Raman , once allies, are now skirmishing over homelessness, housing affordability and how to best prepare for the 2028 Olympics. The race has tightened (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/29/karen-bass-is-back-in-the-race-01140222), despite polls showing deep dissatisfaction with the mayor.
Raman, who narrowly bested Spencer Pratt in the primary, has criticized Bass’ homelessness strategy and her plan to loosen short-term-rental rules (https://www.thesportsexaminer.com/los-angeles-2028-l-a-mayor-bass-proposing-rule-change-to-allow-more-airbnb-rentals-in-2028-motions-on-la28-purchases-reimbursements-headed-to-council/) during the Games. Hollywood is another fault line: Raman vows to bring production jobs back, though she recused herself from four of seven council votes (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2026/10/23/nithya-ramans-answer-to-the-hollywood-question-01133465) on entertainment industry-related measures because her husband works in television. The winner will help lead both the city’s Olympic preparations and its response to Hollywood’s jobs crisis, which has been fomented by years of runaway production (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/08/16/hollywood-film-production-illinois-tax-credits-01037735?utm_medium=activitypub). A Raman victory would mark a sea change at City Hall and thrust her into the national spotlight, inviting comparisons to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — whether or not they hold up (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/09/new-mayoral-challenger-in-los-angeles-draws-mamdani-comparisons-00771033) under close examination.
Liam Dillon: Lots of people are talking about the LA mayor’s race and I’ll add to the chorus, but through the lens of housing. A Raman win combined with the expected victory of Janeese Lewis George as mayor of Washington D.C., would be a boon to the burgeoning nationwide “Left-YIMBY (https://x.com/Janeese4DC/status/2109410845113618690)” movement. Raman, Lewis George and Mamdani all are members of the Democratic Socialists of America and promise to expand protections for tenants as part of their agendas. But at the same time, they’ve embraced the role of the private market in housing development and have pledged to remove zoning restrictions and other municipal barriers to growth — policies favored by pro-growth, Yes In My Backyard activists.
As I’ve written, the idea faces healthy skepticism (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/03/07/mamdani-nithya-raman-housing-socialism-abundance-00817314). One centrist critic calls Left-YIMBYism “capitalism for developers, communism for landlords.” But its supporters believe its potential success could end the left’s housing wars and lead to an enduring, renter-centered political coalition.
Tyler Katzenberger: Will tech’s spending spree in state legislative races pay off? A North Bay Assembly contest between fellow Democrats Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward offers a test: Grow California, funded by crypto executives Chris Larsen and Tim Draper , has cumulatively spent more than $1 million backing Lucan and opposing Elward, labor’s favored candidate. A Lucan win would help validate the industry’s strategy of swaying state politics by spending big in Dem-on-Dem races, while an Elward victory would be a triumph for labor leaders who increasingly find themselves at war with tech interests.
The race also has high stakes for Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas , who ruffled feathers among the Legislature’s Black and Progressive caucuses (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/11/rivas-assembly-senate-endorsements-01144382) by endorsing Lucan, who is seen as the more moderate candidate, over Elward, a Black woman and self-identified progressive.
Lindsey Holden: Proposition 39, California’s voter ID ballot measure, once looked like it might have a real shot. Polling earlier this year suggested the concept was broadly popular (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/05/04/california-democrats-voter-id-00905425), and Democrats were slow to mount an opposition campaign (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/04/californias-fight-against-voter-id-is-a-slow-burn-00905656). But in the months since the primary, voting rights groups, labor, legislative leaders, Gov. Gavin Newsom and his likely successor, Xavier Becerra , all lined up against it (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/24/california-dems-ramp-up-anti-voter-id-fight-01011990), relentlessly yoking the measure to Trump.
The messaging seems to have paid off. The measure is trailing in polls (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-voter-id-measure-falling-short-in-new-poll-01127047), and the president’s ongoing efforts to exert control over California’s elections (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2026/10/15/california-noncitizen-voting-lawsuit-01121542) likely isn’t helping Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio create the bipartisan coalition he would have needed to make it law.
Saqib Rahim: The traditionally low-profile race for insurance commissioner has become a dramatic faceoff this year between an up-and-coming progressive, former Sanders campaigner Jane Kim , and an experienced Sacramento Democrat, state Sen. Ben Allen , whose own mom was displaced by the LA fires. On its face, it’s a classic insider-outsider battle. But it’s also become a debate about government: how extensively the government should intervene when people feel crushed by the cost of living, versus trusting market forces to fix things. It’s a debate Republicans and Democrats are having around America about an issue that is only going to become more urgent on a hotter planet.
Alex Nieves: A handful of Assembly races could help progressives gain ground in a chamber dominated by moderates in recent years. That includes the Orange County district where Sanders-backed candidate Jessie Lopez is challenging fellow Democrat David Penaloza . Lopez, a Santa Ana City Council member and member of the Working Families Party, has garnered endorsements from progressives like Assemblymember Alex Lee and state Sen. Caroline Menjivar , while Penaloza has the support of Rivas and the California Democratic Party. The oil industry has also come out against Lopez, contributing to an independent expenditure committee that’s spent more than $1 million to oppose her.
GOOD MORNING. Happy Monday. Thanks for waking up with California Playbook.

WHO WON THE DAY? Becerra, who spent his final election rally as the headliner among the state’s top Democrats including Newsom, Harris, Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla . It’s a far cry from Becerra’s popularity this time last year, when his gubernatorial campaign was finding no traction.
WHERE’S GAVIN? Holding internal meetings.

By JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason)

POLITICO Named Digiday’s Most Innovative Publisher — Yesterday POLITICO was named 2026 Most Innovative Publisher by Digiday. We are proud of this honor and of the incredible efforts of our team around the world. We also know the credit starts with you, our readers and subscribers.
Everything we have built this year, including our expansions to Australia and Spain, Decoded by POLITICO, the POLITICO Pub and our mobile app, began with the same question: What do the people who count on us need next? Your feedback is how we find the answer, and your trust is what we work to earn every day.
Thank you. We are not finished. There is more coming, and we will keep building it for you.
POLITICO CEO Goli Sheikholeslami and Global Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger
Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks at a campaign rally in support of California Proposition 40 in Los Angeles, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. | Jae C. Hong/AP
DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.

California’s electricity rates are the second-highest in the U.S., behind only Hawaii. Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
By JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason)
10/28/2026 09:00 AM EDT
POLITICO Named Digiday’s Most Innovative Publisher — Yesterday POLITICO was named 2026 Most Innovative Publisher by Digiday. We are proud of this honor and of the incredible efforts of our team around the world. We also know the credit starts with you, our readers and subscribers.
Everything we have built this year, including our expansions to Australia and Spain, Decoded by POLITICO, the POLITICO Pub and our mobile app, began with the same question: What do the people who count on us need next? Your feedback is how we find the answer, and your trust is what we work to earn every day.
Thank you. We are not finished. There is more coming, and we will keep building it for you.
POLITICO CEO Goli Sheikholeslami and Global Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger
Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks at a campaign rally in support of California Proposition 40 in Los Angeles, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. | Jae C. Hong/AP
DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

Or you can text us at ‪ 916-562-0685 ‬‪ — save it as “ CA Playbook ” in your contacts.
WHO WON THE DAY? Prop 40 opponents , who received good news in the PPIC poll.
WHERE’S GAVIN? In Los Angeles, having a fireside chat with California Science Center CEO Jeffrey Rudolph during a media preview of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center.
TOP READS
SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.
Read the full story from Christine Mui and Sean McMinn here (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/28/billionaires-spending-california-wealth-tax-01137778) .
IN THE COURTS
In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman
ELECTION YEAR
Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.

DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”

First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO

Judge J. “The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.

I'm looking at the Prop 42 campaign, which had a huge influx of money in October, mostly from wealthy backers, and is running heavy TV ads about protecting retirement savings. Next I'm weighing the evidence for Yes, starting with the PPIC poll, which shows it ahead 51 to 47.

Now I'm lining up the polls against each other: PPIC has Yes ahead, and the AIMSA poll shows it at 50%, while Berkeley IGS has No slightly ahead and trending down for Yes. I'm also noting the big spending edge and the Yes-favoring prediction markets, but the late-poll pattern of undecideds breaking No on ballot measures is pulling the other way.

Now I'm weighing the No side: the Democratic Party and major newspapers back No, and the "poison pill" framing plus heavy young and Latino turnout could pull voters away from Prop 42. The prediction markets have also dropped sharply in the final week, which points toward No.

Now I'm comparing how PPIC and IGS differ in method: IGS is an online opt-in sample with a larger undecided share, and I'm checking how each poll did on the 2024 props, starting with the school bond and marriage measure.

Now I'm checking how PPIC and IGS did on last cycle's propositions, going through the 2024 results like the rent control and minimum wage measures to see which poll tracked the outcomes more closely.

Now I'm checking how PPIC and IGS fared on the 2020 Prop 22 and Prop 15 results, where PPIC came closer on Prop 22 and both polls overstated Yes on Prop 15.

Now I'm checking how the 2020 propositions played out against the polls: Prop 15 had heavy No spending, and Prop 16 polled 37-50 and finished at 43-57. Prop 19 polled under 50 yet passed narrowly after heavy Yes spending by realtors, which is another case of money pushing a measure past its polling.

Now I'm going back through the 2020 and 2022 propositions, noting how the polls fared against final results, like Prop 27 where the yes side polled around 26% and ended far lower.

Now I'm going through the 2018 propositions, checking how the polls compared with the results on the gas tax repeal, the rent control measure, and the dialysis and property tax transfer measures.

Now I'm going through the 2016 propositions, checking which measures passed or failed, including the marijuana measures and the heavily funded drug pricing initiative.

Now I'm going through the 2016 and 2018 ballot measures, looking at which anti-tax and anti-government initiatives passed or failed, and how much heavy funding on either side moved the results.

Now I'm weighing the spending edge against the opposition: the Yes side has far more money behind it, while the No side gets free coverage from editorials and the Democratic Party. I'm also recalling older measures like Props 26, 218, and 13, which passed, though this one is a different case since the opposition is underfunded.

Now I'm lining up the ballot measures where a lopsided Yes budget went up against little or no organized No spending, like Prop 22 in 2020 and Prop 35 in 2024. Those mostly passed, though the 2022 sports betting fight, where the Yes side was outspent, shows that money can also lose.

Now I'm checking the spending gaps on the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2024 measures, where the side with less money lost most of the time, except for Prop 19 and Prop 24, which passed with little or no opposition money.

Now I'm checking the spending gaps against the outcomes again, noting that Prop 14 passed at 51% on a modest Yes budget, while the 2020 school bond lost at 47% and the 2024 minimum wage measure lost at 49%. Prop 36 passed at 68% on a roughly four-to-one Yes edge, so a large spending advantage tends to win when the measure itself sounds appealing. Prop 42's ballot label, "Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes," reads as a no-new-taxes message, and I'm starting to weigh the fiscal impact line about tax revenues.

Now I'm weighing how the billionaire tax's losing polls (Prop 40 at 42-46% Yes) might pull some opponents of that measure into voting No on Prop 42 as well.

Now I'm checking the IGS and PPIC numbers side by side: Yes on 42 is about even with No on 40 in PPIC, but in IGS it trails, which suggests some Prop 40 opponents are either undecided or leaning No on 42.

Now I'm recalling the usual pattern that undecided voters on ballot measures tend to break No, and I'm planning to pull up the IGS release for its partisan breakdown and what voters think of the poison pill framing.

I'm looking at the Prop 42 campaign, which had a huge influx of money in October, mostly from wealthy backers, and is running heavy TV ads about protecting retirement savings. Next I'm weighing the evidence for Yes, starting with the PPIC poll, which shows it ahead 51 to 47.

Now I'm lining up the polls against each other: PPIC has Yes ahead, and the AIMSA poll shows it at 50%, while Berkeley IGS has No slightly ahead and trending down for Yes. I'm also noting the big spending edge and the Yes-favoring prediction markets, but the late-poll pattern of undecideds breaking No on ballot measures is pulling the other way.

Now I'm weighing the No side: the Democratic Party and major newspapers back No, and the "poison pill" framing plus heavy young and Latino turnout could pull voters away from Prop 42. The prediction markets have also dropped sharply in the final week, which points toward No.

Now I'm comparing how PPIC and IGS differ in method: IGS is an online opt-in sample with a larger undecided share, and I'm checking how each poll did on the 2024 props, starting with the school bond and marriage measure.

Now I'm checking how PPIC and IGS did on last cycle's propositions, going through the 2024 results like the rent control and minimum wage measures to see which poll tracked the outcomes more closely.

Now I'm checking how PPIC and IGS fared on the 2020 Prop 22 and Prop 15 results, where PPIC came closer on Prop 22 and both polls overstated Yes on Prop 15.

Now I'm checking how the 2020 propositions played out against the polls: Prop 15 had heavy No spending, and Prop 16 polled 37-50 and finished at 43-57. Prop 19 polled under 50 yet passed narrowly after heavy Yes spending by realtors, which is another case of money pushing a measure past its polling.

Now I'm going back through the 2020 and 2022 propositions, noting how the polls fared against final results, like Prop 27 where the yes side polled around 26% and ended far lower.

Now I'm going through the 2018 propositions, checking how the polls compared with the results on the gas tax repeal, the rent control measure, and the dialysis and property tax transfer measures.

Now I'm going through the 2016 propositions, checking which measures passed or failed, including the marijuana measures and the heavily funded drug pricing initiative.

Now I'm going through the 2016 and 2018 ballot measures, looking at which anti-tax and anti-government initiatives passed or failed, and how much heavy funding on either side moved the results.

Now I'm weighing the spending edge against the opposition: the Yes side has far more money behind it, while the No side gets free coverage from editorials and the Democratic Party. I'm also recalling older measures like Props 26, 218, and 13, which passed, though this one is a different case since the opposition is underfunded.

Now I'm lining up the ballot measures where a lopsided Yes budget went up against little or no organized No spending, like Prop 22 in 2020 and Prop 35 in 2024. Those mostly passed, though the 2022 sports betting fight, where the Yes side was outspent, shows that money can also lose.

Now I'm checking the spending gaps on the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2024 measures, where the side with less money lost most of the time, except for Prop 19 and Prop 24, which passed with little or no opposition money.

Now I'm checking the spending gaps against the outcomes again, noting that Prop 14 passed at 51% on a modest Yes budget, while the 2020 school bond lost at 47% and the 2024 minimum wage measure lost at 49%. Prop 36 passed at 68% on a roughly four-to-one Yes edge, so a large spending advantage tends to win when the measure itself sounds appealing. Prop 42's ballot label, "Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes," reads as a no-new-taxes message, and I'm starting to weigh the fiscal impact line about tax revenues.

Now I'm recalling the usual pattern that undecided voters on ballot measures tend to break No, and I'm planning to pull up the IGS release for its partisan breakdown and what voters think of the poison pill framing.

Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.
A T-shirt with a campaign message is seen before the start of a rally led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.
From the 2026 Voter Guide
Learn about Proposition 40 and its supporters, opponents, and arguments (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40)
“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.
Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)
PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.

Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.
A T-shirt with a campaign message is seen before the start of a rally led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.
From the 2026 Voter Guide
Learn about Proposition 40 and its supporters, opponents, and arguments (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40)
“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.
Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)
PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.

Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.
A T-shirt with a campaign message is seen before the start of a rally led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.
From the 2026 Voter Guide
Learn about Proposition 40 and its supporters, opponents, and arguments (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40)
“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.
Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)
PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

How this is built
Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm weighing the forecasts: one model puts Prop 42 Yes at 56.9% to pass, the polls sit at 50%, and markets are near 55%. The consensus leans slightly toward Yes, but it's close to a toss-up, so I'm now working out which way to tilt based on the factors the numbers don't capture.

I'm weighing spending against the signals: Yes has about $157M behind it with almost no organized No money, yet the polls are drifting down for Yes, which suggests the "poison pill" argument is landing anyway. The PPIC breakdown splits by party, with Republicans and independents leaning Yes and Democrats leaning No. Early Democratic turnout is also running well ahead of expectations, which would hurt a measure Republicans favor, though the On Point model may already bake that in.

I'm now checking where the Democratic leaders stand on Prop 42, since Newsom backs Yes while the party's other figures may not, and I also want the Labor Federation and CTA positions. Prop 42 is marketed as protecting retirement savings from new taxes, and the ballot label about personal property taxes may pull in low-information voters, though California has passed plenty of tax increases before. I'm also recalling how Prop 65 in 2016 was a countermeasure that lost while its rival passed.

I'm now going through past California ballot measures where an industry counter-measure ran against a rival, looking at how those contests turned out, including the 1988 insurance measures, the 2010 Chamber-backed vote requirement that narrowly passed, and the 1978 Prop 13 fight.

I'm now looking at how Prop 40 voters might split on Prop 42: among those who back Prop 40 and would need to vote No on 42, versus those opposed who might add a Yes on 42 as extra protection. The real question is whether Prop 42 clears 50% on its own.

Working through the Prop 40 splits, I get roughly 43% Yes, 41% No, and 12% undecided on Prop 42, which lines up with the IGS numbers. That means Prop 42 trails the 45% No on Prop 40 by a few points. The undecideds are probably mostly Prop 40 No voters who aren't sure about 42, so I'm wondering which way they'll break.

I'm still weighing the undecided voters on Prop 42, who could go either way depending on how they feel about the billionaire tax and the constitutional change. In the PPIC poll, nearly all No-on-40 voters back Yes on 42, while most Yes-on-40 voters lean No, so the outcome hinges on how many voters end up opposing Prop 40. I want to pin down the market's expected margin on Prop 40 before judging whether Prop 42 can clear 50%.

# Endorsement: Yes on Proposition 42
By The Times Editorial Board
May 18, 2014 12 AM PT
Should government workers and elected officials in cities, counties, water districts, school districts and other local governments be required to do their public business in public?
Should they be required to post meeting agendas and turn over documents on request?
Of course.
It’s a no-brainer.
We shouldn’t need a ballot measure to require them to obey what is already California law.
We shouldn’t have to go to the polls on June 3 to vote for Proposition 42.
We shouldn’t have to — but we do.
The Times strongly endorses Proposition 42.
The measure would amend the state Constitution to prevent lawmakers from suspending portions of the Ralph M. Brown Act requiring adequate public notice of local government meetings, and portions of the Public Records Act requiring that documents be available for public inspection.

I'm weighing the forecasts: one model puts Prop 42 Yes at 56.9% to pass, the polls sit at 50%, and markets are near 55%. The consensus leans slightly toward Yes, but it's close to a toss-up, so I'm now working out which way to tilt based on the factors the numbers don't capture.

I'm weighing spending against the signals: Yes has about $157M behind it with almost no organized No money, yet the polls are drifting down for Yes, which suggests the "poison pill" argument is landing anyway. The PPIC breakdown splits by party, with Republicans and independents leaning Yes and Democrats leaning No. Early Democratic turnout is also running well ahead of expectations, which would hurt a measure Republicans favor, though the On Point model may already bake that in.

I'm now checking where the Democratic leaders stand on Prop 42, since Newsom backs Yes while the party's other figures may not, and I also want the Labor Federation and CTA positions. Prop 42 is marketed as protecting retirement savings from new taxes, and the ballot label about personal property taxes may pull in low-information voters, though California has passed plenty of tax increases before. I'm also recalling how Prop 65 in 2016 was a countermeasure that lost while its rival passed.

I'm now going through past California ballot measures where an industry counter-measure ran against a rival, looking at how those contests turned out, including the 1988 insurance measures, the 2010 Chamber-backed vote requirement that narrowly passed, and the 1978 Prop 13 fight.

I'm now looking at how Prop 40 voters might split on Prop 42: among those who back Prop 40 and would need to vote No on 42, versus those opposed who might add a Yes on 42 as extra protection. The real question is whether Prop 42 clears 50% on its own.

Working through the Prop 40 splits, I get roughly 43% Yes, 41% No, and 12% undecided on Prop 42, which lines up with the IGS numbers. That means Prop 42 trails the 45% No on Prop 40 by a few points. The undecideds are probably mostly Prop 40 No voters who aren't sure about 42, so I'm wondering which way they'll break.

I'm still weighing the undecided voters on Prop 42, who could go either way depending on how they feel about the billionaire tax and the constitutional change. In the PPIC poll, nearly all No-on-40 voters back Yes on 42, while most Yes-on-40 voters lean No, so the outcome hinges on how many voters end up opposing Prop 40. I want to pin down the market's expected margin on Prop 40 before judging whether Prop 42 can clear 50%.

I'm checking the Prop 40 margin market to see how far it's expected to fail, since that shapes how many No-on-40 voters might still vote No on 42. Some of those voters will split off, and some Yes-on-40 voters may still back 42 out of confusion over the retirement-savings pitch.

I'm comparing past California counter-measure fights, noting that industry countermeasures usually draw fewer Yes votes than the main measure they oppose, as with Prop 65 in 2016, though its environmental-fund appeal makes it an imperfect match. I'm also checking the 2022 Props 26 and 27 pair, which both failed, and the 2024 Props 33 and 34 result, where the targeted measure passed while rent control lost, though that's not an exact parallel either.

I'm running through more past California countermeasures, noting that the ones where industry pushed a rival measure, like the 1990 Big Green fight and the 2005 drug discount pair, both lost. Prop 42 doesn't present itself as a countermeasure, though, but as a standalone protection against new taxes, so that comparison only goes so far. I'm also turning to how California voters have treated anti-tax constitutional changes lately, and I'm going to check the Prop 43 situation next.

I'm checking how Prop 43 landed, since it was placed by the Legislature as part of a deal and is trailing badly, and Prop 41 is also trailing in the 38-48% range. Prop 42 looks about five points ahead of Prop 41, probably thanks to its more appealing message and heavier funding. I'm now considering whether measures usually lose support as the campaign goes on, which would bear on the final Yes share for Prop 42.

I'm noting that the No side is picking up ground in both the PPIC and IGS polls between September and October, with Yes slipping in one and holding flat in the other. The election is November 3, and roughly half the ballots will likely arrive in the final stretch, so if that No drift keeps going for another week or two, Prop 42 could drop below where it stands now.

I'm now weighing whether the Yes side's late spending and the markets' 55-57% Yes estimate hold up, since prediction markets on ballot measures are thin and the On Point model's 54.2% prior rests on comparable measures while the polls average 50%. I want to check how PPIC's final poll has held up against past results for measures that were narrowly ahead in PPIC.

Now I'm listing the PPIC October 2024 results against the actual outcomes for each proposition, checking how close those early readings came.

I'm pulling up PPIC's October 2022 results next, comparing their readings for Props 1, 26, 27, and 30 against the actual outcomes, and they look like they tracked fairly well. I'm also checking the 2020 round, where the early readings for Props 14, 15, and 16 were looser, with Prop 15 failing narrowly.

Now I'm going through PPIC's October 2018 readings against the actual results, with the bonds and measures like Prop 3 and Prop 10 running close to the final tallies.

I'm checking how PPIC's past October readings compared to actual results, and they usually land within about 3 to 5 points, so a 51% Yes reading for Prop 42 could end up anywhere from roughly 46% to 56%. I'm also going through IGS's final polls from 2020 to 2024, where the misses were uneven, like Prop 22 coming in far above its poll and Prop 27 far below.

I'm weighing the IGS undecideds against the PPIC numbers, and depending on how the 12% gets split, Prop 42 lands anywhere from about 47% to 51% Yes. Averaging the adjusted PPIC and IGS figures puts it near 49%, close to where On Point's 50% sits. Given that, I'd call it a coin flip, and I want to see whether endorsements or newspaper editorial boards tilt it either way.

I'm noting which editorial boards have endorsed and which have not, and that the LA Times has no endorsement yet as of September 30. I'm also listing the main opponents: the state Democratic Party, the Labor Federation, several unions, and the League of Women Voters.

I'm checking the opponents and supporters list, which includes CNA. Then I'm weighing Prop 42's chances against Prop 40, since the two are close to mirror images and likely move together. The polls put Prop 42 near 50%, which is what I'm reconciling against the No on 40 numbers.

I'm weighing three factors for Prop 42: its late spot on a long ballot with 14 measures, which tends to push voters toward No; the general willingness of California voters to back taxes on the wealthy, which doesn't carry over neatly since Prop 42 is framed around protecting ordinary people's retirement savings; and awareness of its poison-pill nature, which DiCamillo found drives opposition as the election nears.

I'm weighing the factors that could tip Prop 42: heavy Yes spending that mostly hasn't moved the numbers, a Democratic-leaning electorate with high enthusiasm, and Newsom's endorsement, which may win over some moderate Democrats.

I'm checking whether the Democratic Party's official slate, which says No, changes how undecided voters will break. Ballot measures usually break No when voters are unsure, but since Prop 42 is framed as protecting against taxes, undecideds might lean Yes instead. I'm leaning toward it being roughly even, and I'm now looking for IGS poll numbers on Prop 42 broken down by party.

Proposition 42: Personal Property and State Taxes
Proposition 42: Personal Property and State Taxes
Proposition 42: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes And Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act
Summary
Proposition 42 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0039A1 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0039A1%20%28CA%20Residency%20Act%20%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 42 amends the California Constitution by adding Article VIII, Sections 1 through 9.
Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets (e.g. pensions, stocks, or retirement accounts) and tangible or intangible personal property would not be allowed.
Proposition 42 also prohibits retroactive taxes that authorize a tax on conduct, activities, or status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date of the state law or constitution. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 (Billionaire Wealth Tax) on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future, making it somewhat harder to raise revenue through taxes. It is unclear how much future revenues would be reduced.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
