WHERE’S GAVIN? In Los Angeles, having a fireside chat with California Science Center CEO Jeffrey Rudolph during a media preview of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center.
TOP READS
SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.
Read the full story from Christine Mui and Sean McMinn here (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/28/billionaires-spending-california-wealth-tax-01137778) .
IN THE COURTS
In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman
ELECTION YEAR
Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.
LOS ANGELES
Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks during a campaign event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Sylmar, California. | William Liang/AP
POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. California’s electricity rates are the second-highest in the U.S., behind only Hawaii. Read last night’s California Currents (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-currents/2026/10/27/ramans-electric-closing-message-01137445) to see how both campaigns are trying to navigate energy affordability angst ahead of Election Day.

UCLA SUIT — For the second time this month, the University of California has asked a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit by the Department of Justice alleging that UCLA failed to properly address antisemitic incidents during protests over Israel’s war against Hamas.
In a motion filed later Monday, UC officials acknowledged that “there is no question that some University employees were exposed to antisemitism on campus” but called the Trump administration’s claims of a campus overrun by it “flawed,” Eric He reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/uc-seeks-to-dismiss-another-doj-antisemitism-lawsuit-01136943).

I'm looking at the Prop 42 campaign, which had a huge influx of money in October, mostly from wealthy backers, and is running heavy TV ads about protecting retirement savings. Next I'm weighing the evidence for Yes, starting with the PPIC poll, which shows it ahead 51 to 47.

Now I'm lining up the polls against each other: PPIC has Yes ahead, and the AIMSA poll shows it at 50%, while Berkeley IGS has No slightly ahead and trending down for Yes. I'm also noting the big spending edge and the Yes-favoring prediction markets, but the late-poll pattern of undecideds breaking No on ballot measures is pulling the other way.

Now I'm weighing the No side: the Democratic Party and major newspapers back No, and the "poison pill" framing plus heavy young and Latino turnout could pull voters away from Prop 42. The prediction markets have also dropped sharply in the final week, which points toward No.

Now I'm comparing how PPIC and IGS differ in method: IGS is an online opt-in sample with a larger undecided share, and I'm checking how each poll did on the 2024 props, starting with the school bond and marriage measure.

Now I'm checking how PPIC and IGS did on last cycle's propositions, going through the 2024 results like the rent control and minimum wage measures to see which poll tracked the outcomes more closely.

Now I'm checking how PPIC and IGS fared on the 2020 Prop 22 and Prop 15 results, where PPIC came closer on Prop 22 and both polls overstated Yes on Prop 15.

Now I'm checking how the 2020 propositions played out against the polls: Prop 15 had heavy No spending, and Prop 16 polled 37-50 and finished at 43-57. Prop 19 polled under 50 yet passed narrowly after heavy Yes spending by realtors, which is another case of money pushing a measure past its polling.

Now I'm going back through the 2020 and 2022 propositions, noting how the polls fared against final results, like Prop 27 where the yes side polled around 26% and ended far lower.

Now I'm going through the 2018 propositions, checking how the polls compared with the results on the gas tax repeal, the rent control measure, and the dialysis and property tax transfer measures.

Now I'm going through the 2016 propositions, checking which measures passed or failed, including the marijuana measures and the heavily funded drug pricing initiative.

Now I'm going through the 2016 and 2018 ballot measures, looking at which anti-tax and anti-government initiatives passed or failed, and how much heavy funding on either side moved the results.

Now I'm weighing the spending edge against the opposition: the Yes side has far more money behind it, while the No side gets free coverage from editorials and the Democratic Party. I'm also recalling older measures like Props 26, 218, and 13, which passed, though this one is a different case since the opposition is underfunded.

Now I'm lining up the ballot measures where a lopsided Yes budget went up against little or no organized No spending, like Prop 22 in 2020 and Prop 35 in 2024. Those mostly passed, though the 2022 sports betting fight, where the Yes side was outspent, shows that money can also lose.

Now I'm checking the spending gaps on the 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2024 measures, where the side with less money lost most of the time, except for Prop 19 and Prop 24, which passed with little or no opposition money.

Now I'm checking the spending gaps against the outcomes again, noting that Prop 14 passed at 51% on a modest Yes budget, while the 2020 school bond lost at 47% and the 2024 minimum wage measure lost at 49%. Prop 36 passed at 68% on a roughly four-to-one Yes edge, so a large spending advantage tends to win when the measure itself sounds appealing. Prop 42's ballot label, "Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes," reads as a no-new-taxes message, and I'm starting to weigh the fiscal impact line about tax revenues.

Now I'm weighing how the billionaire tax's losing polls (Prop 40 at 42-46% Yes) might pull some opponents of that measure into voting No on Prop 42 as well.

Now I'm checking the IGS and PPIC numbers side by side: Yes on 42 is about even with No on 40 in PPIC, but in IGS it trails, which suggests some Prop 40 opponents are either undecided or leaning No on 42.

Now I'm recalling the usual pattern that undecided voters on ballot measures tend to break No, and I'm planning to pull up the IGS release for its partisan breakdown and what voters think of the poison pill framing.

Is California’s Proposed Billionaire Tax in Trouble? New Polls Find Bad News
Two public nonpartisan surveys show Proposition 40 trailing in the final days of voting. Meanwhile, an initiative to require voter ID in California is losing by double digits.
Oct 29, 2026
Marisa Lagos (https://www.kqed.org/author/mlagos)
U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) speaks at a rally dubbed "Ballots Over Billionaires" at The Novo on Oct. 5, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders joined Khanna for the event in support of Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of approximately 200 California billionaires, with most of the revenue intended to offset cuts to Medi-Cal and other healthcare services. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
A proposal to tax California’s billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12106033/the-political-calculus-behind-newsoms-opposition-to-californias-billionaire-tax) to fund healthcare is trailing in two public, nonpartisan polls released this week, surveys that also found strong opposition to a separate ballot measure that would require voters to show identification at the polls.
Proposition 40 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40), which would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the overall wealth of the state’s billionaires, was tracking below the majority needed to pass in polls from both UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. With days left to vote in the Nov. 3 midterm election, IGS found just 8% of likely voters still undecided on the measure, which billionaires (https://www.kqed.org/news/12104645/sf-billionaire-chris-larsen-on-ai-this-is-an-incredibly-dangerous-moment) have spent more than $300 million to defeat.
Proposition 39 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39), the voter ID initiative, was also trailing by 20 points in the IGS poll, with just 37% of likely voters saying they were voting yes and 5% undecided. PPIC’s poll found slightly stronger support for the measure, but still had it losing.
Support for Proposition 40 appears to be slipping heading into Election Day. Last month’s PPIC poll had a slim majority in favor before the slide this month.
But in the IGS poll released this week, half of likely voters said they will vote no on Proposition 40, while 42% said they are voting yes. That’s a shift from last month, when the IGS poll found 42% of voters against the measure and 45% backing it.
A T-shirt with a campaign message is seen before the start of a rally led by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act at The Wiltern in Los Angeles, on Feb. 18, 2026. Sanders is seeking the support of California voters for a November ballot initiative of an emergency tax on billionaires to help the state’s healthcare system. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
Mark DiCamillo, director of the IGS Poll, said the No on Proposition 40 side is clearly benefiting from the huge amounts of money being poured into defeating the wealth tax.
“A well-funded no side campaign usually has the advantage over yes campaigns, just because all they have to do is raise doubts,” he said.
The poll found Proposition 40 backed by strong majorities of Democrats and voters under 40, and opposed by Republicans and voters over 50. Independents are split.
DiCamillo said the disparity between how younger and older voters view the proposed tax is indicative of a growing split that did not used to exist among the California electorate.
From the 2026 Voter Guide
Learn about Proposition 40 and its supporters, opponents, and arguments (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-40)
“The generational divide is growing over time, just because the younger set is having a hard time. They can’t afford a house, they can’t reach the American dream,” he said.
“Those are the segments that are now migrating to the Democratic socialists…. They really don’t like the disparity in wealth.”
The fate of the proposed wealth tax will not swing solely on Proposition 40.
Both polls also showed close contests in Propositions 41 and 42, measures put on the ballot by billionaires with language that would nullify the tax if they pass with more votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 41 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-41) would require ongoing audits of state programs that are funded by “special” taxes — those earmarked for a specific purpose. It also would make any new special taxes subject to the state’s existing spending limit. Proposition 42 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-42) would prohibit new taxes on financial assets — such as stocks — and other personal property, and also prohibit most retroactive taxes.
While IGS’s survey showed Propositions 41 and 42 slightly ahead, DiCamillo noted they also found double-digit percentages of likely voters still undecided — and those who have moved since IGS’s September survey have largely turned against the billionaire-backed measures.
“The no side has gained 11 [points] while the yes side is static,” DiCamillo said of Proposition 42.
Proposition 39, the voter ID measure placed on the ballot by Republican lawmakers, has also lost ground since IGS’s poll last month, with the no side gaining 7 percentage points. The survey found Republicans are the only group backing the measure. Likely voters who list no party preference are against it by a 15-point margin in the IGS poll, and majorities of voters in nearly all subgroups — age, race and gender — are opposed.
Sen. Tony Strickland speaks at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, for a press conference highlighting voter signatures in favor of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)
PPIC found similar opposition: That survey has Proposition 39 down by 17 points, with 58% of likely voters saying they will vote no.
DiCamillo said voters appear to be linking the voter ID measure to President Donald Trump’s push for changes to election laws, which are unpopular with Democrats and independents.
“I think Trump is a factor,” he said. “That really is the winning argument: You go after Trump.”
PPIC also polled on Proposition 45 (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-45), the ballot measure written by the California Chamber of Commerce to speed up environmental reviews of construction projects. The survey found likely voters split on the changes to the California Environmental Quality Act, with 46% saying they are voting yes and 50% voting no.
The IGS poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 19-25, and included 2,787 registered voters. The PPIC poll was conducted online in English and Spanish from Oct. 16-22 and included 1,728 California adult residents.
Both polls have a sampling error of plus or minus 3%.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

I'm weighing the forecasts: one model puts Prop 42 Yes at 56.9% to pass, the polls sit at 50%, and markets are near 55%. The consensus leans slightly toward Yes, but it's close to a toss-up, so I'm now working out which way to tilt based on the factors the numbers don't capture.

I'm weighing spending against the signals: Yes has about $157M behind it with almost no organized No money, yet the polls are drifting down for Yes, which suggests the "poison pill" argument is landing anyway. The PPIC breakdown splits by party, with Republicans and independents leaning Yes and Democrats leaning No. Early Democratic turnout is also running well ahead of expectations, which would hurt a measure Republicans favor, though the On Point model may already bake that in.

I'm now checking where the Democratic leaders stand on Prop 42, since Newsom backs Yes while the party's other figures may not, and I also want the Labor Federation and CTA positions. Prop 42 is marketed as protecting retirement savings from new taxes, and the ballot label about personal property taxes may pull in low-information voters, though California has passed plenty of tax increases before. I'm also recalling how Prop 65 in 2016 was a countermeasure that lost while its rival passed.

I'm now going through past California ballot measures where an industry counter-measure ran against a rival, looking at how those contests turned out, including the 1988 insurance measures, the 2010 Chamber-backed vote requirement that narrowly passed, and the 1978 Prop 13 fight.

I'm now looking at how Prop 40 voters might split on Prop 42: among those who back Prop 40 and would need to vote No on 42, versus those opposed who might add a Yes on 42 as extra protection. The real question is whether Prop 42 clears 50% on its own.

Working through the Prop 40 splits, I get roughly 43% Yes, 41% No, and 12% undecided on Prop 42, which lines up with the IGS numbers. That means Prop 42 trails the 45% No on Prop 40 by a few points. The undecideds are probably mostly Prop 40 No voters who aren't sure about 42, so I'm wondering which way they'll break.

I'm still weighing the undecided voters on Prop 42, who could go either way depending on how they feel about the billionaire tax and the constitutional change. In the PPIC poll, nearly all No-on-40 voters back Yes on 42, while most Yes-on-40 voters lean No, so the outcome hinges on how many voters end up opposing Prop 40. I want to pin down the market's expected margin on Prop 40 before judging whether Prop 42 can clear 50%.

I'm checking the Prop 40 margin market to see how far it's expected to fail, since that shapes how many No-on-40 voters might still vote No on 42. Some of those voters will split off, and some Yes-on-40 voters may still back 42 out of confusion over the retirement-savings pitch.

I'm comparing past California counter-measure fights, noting that industry countermeasures usually draw fewer Yes votes than the main measure they oppose, as with Prop 65 in 2016, though its environmental-fund appeal makes it an imperfect match. I'm also checking the 2022 Props 26 and 27 pair, which both failed, and the 2024 Props 33 and 34 result, where the targeted measure passed while rent control lost, though that's not an exact parallel either.

I'm running through more past California countermeasures, noting that the ones where industry pushed a rival measure, like the 1990 Big Green fight and the 2005 drug discount pair, both lost. Prop 42 doesn't present itself as a countermeasure, though, but as a standalone protection against new taxes, so that comparison only goes so far. I'm also turning to how California voters have treated anti-tax constitutional changes lately, and I'm going to check the Prop 43 situation next.

I'm checking how Prop 43 landed, since it was placed by the Legislature as part of a deal and is trailing badly, and Prop 41 is also trailing in the 38-48% range. Prop 42 looks about five points ahead of Prop 41, probably thanks to its more appealing message and heavier funding. I'm now considering whether measures usually lose support as the campaign goes on, which would bear on the final Yes share for Prop 42.

I'm noting that the No side is picking up ground in both the PPIC and IGS polls between September and October, with Yes slipping in one and holding flat in the other. The election is November 3, and roughly half the ballots will likely arrive in the final stretch, so if that No drift keeps going for another week or two, Prop 42 could drop below where it stands now.

I'm now weighing whether the Yes side's late spending and the markets' 55-57% Yes estimate hold up, since prediction markets on ballot measures are thin and the On Point model's 54.2% prior rests on comparable measures while the polls average 50%. I want to check how PPIC's final poll has held up against past results for measures that were narrowly ahead in PPIC.

Now I'm listing the PPIC October 2024 results against the actual outcomes for each proposition, checking how close those early readings came.

I'm pulling up PPIC's October 2022 results next, comparing their readings for Props 1, 26, 27, and 30 against the actual outcomes, and they look like they tracked fairly well. I'm also checking the 2020 round, where the early readings for Props 14, 15, and 16 were looser, with Prop 15 failing narrowly.

Now I'm going through PPIC's October 2018 readings against the actual results, with the bonds and measures like Prop 3 and Prop 10 running close to the final tallies.

I'm checking how PPIC's past October readings compared to actual results, and they usually land within about 3 to 5 points, so a 51% Yes reading for Prop 42 could end up anywhere from roughly 46% to 56%. I'm also going through IGS's final polls from 2020 to 2024, where the misses were uneven, like Prop 22 coming in far above its poll and Prop 27 far below.

I'm weighing the IGS undecideds against the PPIC numbers, and depending on how the 12% gets split, Prop 42 lands anywhere from about 47% to 51% Yes. Averaging the adjusted PPIC and IGS figures puts it near 49%, close to where On Point's 50% sits. Given that, I'd call it a coin flip, and I want to see whether endorsements or newspaper editorial boards tilt it either way.

I'm checking whether the Prop 42 endorsements and editorial boards lean one way, starting with the Sacramento Bee and the San Diego paper, then the Labor Federation's and CTA's stances. I also want to weigh the early-vote numbers, since a Democratic-heavy electorate would weigh against a measure that leans Republican.

Checking the endorsements and editorial stances on Prop 42 now.

I'm noting which editorial boards have endorsed and which have not, and that the LA Times has no endorsement yet as of September 30. I'm also listing the main opponents: the state Democratic Party, the Labor Federation, several unions, and the League of Women Voters.

I'm checking the opponents and supporters list, which includes CNA. Then I'm weighing Prop 42's chances against Prop 40, since the two are close to mirror images and likely move together. The polls put Prop 42 near 50%, which is what I'm reconciling against the No on 40 numbers.

I'm weighing three factors for Prop 42: its late spot on a long ballot with 14 measures, which tends to push voters toward No; the general willingness of California voters to back taxes on the wealthy, which doesn't carry over neatly since Prop 42 is framed around protecting ordinary people's retirement savings; and awareness of its poison-pill nature, which DiCamillo found drives opposition as the election nears.

I'm weighing the factors that could tip Prop 42: heavy Yes spending that mostly hasn't moved the numbers, a Democratic-leaning electorate with high enthusiasm, and Newsom's endorsement, which may win over some moderate Democrats.

I'm checking whether the Democratic Party's official slate, which says No, changes how undecided voters will break. Ballot measures usually break No when voters are unsure, but since Prop 42 is framed as protecting against taxes, undecideds might lean Yes instead. I'm leaning toward it being roughly even, and I'm now looking for IGS poll numbers on Prop 42 broken down by party.

Proposition 42: Personal Property and State Taxes
Proposition 42: Personal Property and State Taxes
Proposition 42: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes And Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act
Summary
Proposition 42 was placed on the ballot by petition signatures to amend the California Constitution. It began as Initiative #25-0039A1 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0039A1%20%28CA%20Residency%20Act%20%29.pdf) , filed with the California Attorney General’s Office. Prop. 42 amends the California Constitution by adding Article VIII, Sections 1 through 9.
Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets (e.g. pensions, stocks, or retirement accounts) and tangible or intangible personal property would not be allowed.
Proposition 42 also prohibits retroactive taxes that authorize a tax on conduct, activities, or status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date of the state law or constitution. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 (Billionaire Wealth Tax) on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future, making it somewhat harder to raise revenue through taxes. It is unclear how much future revenues would be reduced.
What your vote means (LAO Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

Supporters argue that Proposition 42 protects Californians' retirement funds, savings, and personal assets from new state taxes and prevents unexpected retroactive tax hikes.

I'm going through who has endorsed Prop 42. On the yes side that's the state Republican and Libertarian parties, business and taxpayer groups, firefighters, building trades, PORAC, Governor Newsom, and several newspapers. The no side includes the Democratic, Green, and Peace & Freedom parties, the ACLU chapters, the League of Women Voters, and SPU.

Now I'm working through the rest of the endorsement list, the no side and the CTA position, which is blank. Then I'm checking the past gas-tax and property-tax measures that had this same party split and seeing how they turned out.

I'm checking the past measures with a split like this one, and the ones that passed, Props 22, 36, and 26, all had heavy Yes funding and a popular message. Prop 42's retirement-savings framing looks strong too, but its polling is weaker than Props 22 and 36 were at this point.

I'm comparing the polling against Prop 22's outcome, where the result beat PPIC by a few points and IGS by about twelve, which would put Prop 42 near 53 to 55 percent. Then I'm checking Prop 15, where heavy business spending pulled the late vote toward No and it finished around 48 percent, close to where the polls had it.

I'm estimating what Prop 42 would get under typical undecided-breaks-No behavior, which puts the IGS number around 44 to 46 percent Yes and PPIC near 51 to 52. I'm also recalling Prop 19 from 2020, where Yes spending was heavy and opposition was light, and its result ended around 51 percent.

I'm weighing whether heavy one-sided Yes spending could push the undecideds toward Yes, as it did for Props 19, 14, and 22. That would move the IGS number up toward 49 or 50 percent, since this No campaign is comparatively thin on money even though it has earned media and party and labor backing.

I'm weighing how the No campaign gained eleven points in the IGS poll while Yes stayed flat, which suggests undecided voters are moving toward the No message. The PPIC numbers show a smaller shift, with Yes slipping a few points and No rising a few, so the two polls disagree on how much momentum there is. I'm now looking at how the electorate's party makeup might shape the final result.

I'm running the electorate math here: with a more Democratic likely-voter mix, the yes share drops to about 50%, roughly where the PPIC numbers already sit. I'm now testing what happens if Democrats shift further toward No.

I'm working out the Yes share under a few Democratic turnout scenarios, which lands around 48 to 51.5 percent depending on how Democrats vote. So the result depends mostly on how many Democrats end up voting Yes. Looking at the early-vote composition, I'm now checking how the late electorate might differ.

I'm checking whether the Prop 40 Yes share can be inferred from the Kalshi market on Prop 42 versus Prop 40, since that would tell me how the two measures are expected to compare.

I'm weighing the Prop 40 numbers next: its Yes share sits around 45%, so the No side is near 55%. For Prop 42 to pass, it would need almost all of those opponents to stay out while still picking up some Prop 40 supporters, and even a net leakage of about 5 points would only bring it to roughly 50%. I'm also comparing how the two measures moved from September to October in each poll, to see whether they tracked together.

I'm noticing that No on Prop 42 rose 11 points in the IGS poll, the same kind of shift as Prop 40, which points to undecided voters defaulting to No across the ballot. The PPIC numbers for the other measures, roughly 39 to 45 percent Yes, look similar.

I'm comparing how past contested measures finished against their October PPIC numbers: Props 36, 1, 30, 27, and 26 mostly landed a little lower than the Yes share polled, and Prop 15 came in near 48% after polling at 49%. That pattern suggests Prop 42's PPIC figure of 51% could slip a bit by the final count.

I'm checking whether PPIC's Yes numbers have tended to run high on contested measures, and it looks like they haven't consistently overshot, usually landing within a few points. Next I'm trying to recall the IGS late-October 2024 numbers for the measures on that ballot and how their Yes shares compared with the final results.

I'm recalling the IGS October 2024 numbers for the props on that ballot, which seem to have run several points under their final Yes shares, suggesting undecideds broke Yes or split. I'm not confident in those recollections, so I want to check them against a search before leaning on them.

I'm pulling the calibration figures from the IGS final polls for 2020. Prop 22 stands out: the poll had it at 46-42 with 12 undecided, and it came in at 58.6% Yes, well above the poll's lead, which I'd attribute to the heavy Yes spending. Props 15, 16 and 21 landed close to or below their poll margins.

Checking the 2024 IGS finals next: Prop 32 came in at 49.3% Yes against a poll of 47-39, Prop 33 at 40.0% against 35-45, and Prop 36 at 68.4% against 60-25. Across these cases the Yes result usually landed above the poll's Yes share. I'm now working out each prop's two-party Yes share in the poll to see whether the undecideds broke toward Yes or No.

I'm applying the usual No-shift of roughly 2 to 4 points to Prop 42's poll share, which puts it around 45 to 47%, and a Prop 22-style Yes shift would push it near 55%. I'm also starting to check the PPIC October 2020 calibration figures against their two-party shares.

I'm now checking the PPIC October polls for 2024 and 2022 against their two-party shares, with Prop 32 at 44-54 landing at 49.3% and a Yes shift of about 4 points. I'm also going through the 2022 Props 1, 26, 27 and 30 to see how their results compare to the poll figures.

I'm working out whether Prop 42 looks more like Prop 22, where heavy Yes spending pulled the result up, or like Props 15 and 32, where late movement went No. The two polls average to a two-party Yes share near 50%, which points to a small No shift, unless the Prop 22 pattern holds and pushes it toward 53% or more.

I'm looking at how the Prop 22 Yes campaign framed its message around drivers keeping their flexibility, which won it support despite Democratic opposition. Prop 42 seems to run a similar playbook, with firefighters and teachers in the Yes ads and heavy spending on the Yes side, though the No side is much thinner.

I'm comparing Prop 42 to Prop 22: both are heavily funded Yes campaigns with sympathetic messengers and Democratic opposition, so the Prop 22 pattern is a real possibility. I'm also looking at Prop 19 and Prop 14 from 2020 as other comparisons, though I don't think IGS polled Prop 19.

I'm comparing Prop 42 against past anti-tax and property measures, noting that Prop 218 passed at 56.6% in 1996 while the 2006 and 2008 eminent domain measures failed. The point is that Howard Jarvis-style campaigns with bigger funding don't reliably win in California, which weighs against assuming a Prop 22-style result for Prop 42.

I'm weighing how Prop 42's roughly $157M Yes war chest compares to Prop 22's, and whether the anti-wealth-tax climate, fueled by Brin's money on both sides of Prop 40, makes voters more receptive to the Yes message.

I'm weighing whether Prop 42's Yes share should track the No share on Prop 40, since voters who opposed the wealth-tax expansion would plausibly back a measure framed as protecting against it. The PPIC and IGS numbers put Yes on 42 somewhere between 43 and 51, so I'm checking the Kalshi market for Prop 40's expected vote share next.

Tracking California Proposition 40 wealth tax odds
California’s billionaire wealth-tax initiative was certified for the November 3, 2026 statewide ballot on June 25 as Proposition 40 , officially titled “Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.” The active prediction markets now price whether voters will approve the measure—not whether it will reach the ballot. See the California Secretary of State’s qualified-measures list (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures) and official Proposition 40 voter guide (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40.pdf).
The tracker above compares live prices from Kalshi (https://defirate.com/prediction-markets/kalshi/) and Polymarket Global (https://defirate.com/prediction-markets/polymarket/). DeFi Rate aggregates first-party exchange data. Venue-level prices and activity are shown separately because the platforms report volume on different bases.
If you want to trade the Proposition 40 outcome rather than only follow its odds, compare political betting sites (https://defirate.com/prediction-markets/politics/) for ballot-measure coverage, costs and access.
What to watch before you trade
Voter opinion: Watch California-specific polling that asks about Proposition 40’s actual ballot language rather than wealth taxes in general.
Campaign activity: Endorsements, fundraising, advertising and the official arguments for and against the measure can affect voter awareness and market pricing. Our October 15, 2026 report examined Proposition 40’s polling and campaign-finance divide (https://defirate.com/news/california-wealth-tax-chances-low/); its quoted market prices are a dated snapshot, not the live odds above.
Competing measures: The official voter guide says Proposition 41 or 42 could prevent Proposition 40 from taking effect if either passes and receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40. Compare California propositions 41 and 42 (https://defirate.com/odds/california-props/) with Proposition 40 on the full ballot-measure board.
Contract rules: Kalshi and Polymarket define resolution and early-determination procedures differently. Read the exact venue rules before trading.
Liquidity and spread: Compare bid-ask spreads and venue-level activity rather than relying only on the aggregated probability.
Overview and key details of Proposition 40
Proposition 40 exceeded the 874,641-valid-signature requirement, became eligible on June 17 and was certified on June 25. It would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on covered assets above $1 billion for taxpayers who were California residents on January 1, 2026. Covered assets include businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property. Real property and certain pensions and retirement accounts are excluded.
Payment timing: The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers could spread payments over five years at an additional cost.
Revenue use: Ninety percent would go to public health-care services; the remainder would support education, food assistance and tax administration. The revenue could not replace existing funding for those purposes.
Fiscal estimate: The Legislative Analyst’s Office says the measure would probably raise tens of billions of dollars temporarily, while behavioral responses could reduce ongoing state income-tax revenue by less than $1 billion per year.
Election: California voters decide the measure on November 3, 2026.
Political debate
Supporters—including the California Democratic Party, which endorsed Proposition 40 in August—argue that a one-time tax on billionaires would provide substantial funding for health care and other public services. Governor Gavin Newsom opposes the measure. Other opponents argue that valuation would be difficult, that affected taxpayers could change residency or investment decisions, and that California could lose future income-tax revenue. The official voter guide contains the state’s fiscal analysis and the formal arguments submitted by each side.

Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down

# Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.*** The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

# Your last-minute guide to Propositions 40, 41, 42: The billionaire battle
## Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes.
But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound.
And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
**The basics**
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026.
It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
### Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.

The Yes on 42 campaign is using Newsom's name in its materials, with a "Join Gov. Newsom in voting YES on 42" graphic. Next I want to weigh how much of the Yes vote would come from Republicans and independents versus Democrats, and I'm starting a more careful estimate of the 2026 California midterm electorate by party registration, using the 2022 midterm as a reference.

I'm working through the 2026 turnout estimate by registration, using the 2022 and 2018 midterms as reference points. I'm also checking PPIC's October numbers by party, where independents likely means decline-to-state voters, and the weighted Yes share lands near the 51% they reported. Adjusting for a bit more late movement toward Republicans, the Yes share still looks to be around the low 50s.

I'm checking how the party breakdown lines up with the topline numbers. The PPIC and IGS figures land around 49–51% Yes, and the late shift toward Republicans pushes it a little lower. I'm weighing that against the money behind the campaign, which points the other way.

I'm recomputing the poll average from only the October surveys: weighting IGS and PPIC by sample size gives about 49%, and the full set with recency weighting lifts it to about 50%. Next I'm weighing whether to fold in the earlier comparable-measure prior, which sits higher.

I'm checking the Prop 22 comparison now: which earlier measures would produce that 54.2% prior. Prop 19 polled around 51%, so the match isn't clean. Given only the October polls I land near 49%, which leans toward No, and the trend points the same way. The heavy spending argues for Yes, though, and I want to test whether that offsets the polls by looking at cases where big Yes campaigns still lost.

I'm now checking past cases where heavy Yes spending either carried or failed a measure: Prop 27 in 2022 lost badly, but it faced heavy opposition, so it doesn't isolate the effect. I'm looking at measures with big Yes campaigns and little organized No money, like Props 19, 14, 35, and 34, to see how they polled.

I'm comparing Prop 1 from 2024, which polled strongly for Yes but passed narrowly despite its funding edge, with Prop 53 from 2016, where a large No campaign beat a small Yes one. Those cases show spending doesn't reliably track the result, so the mixed evidence means I'm not reading much into the money here.

I'm now looking at how younger and Latino voters might shift the result: they lean No on Prop 42, and if their turnout rises, that could hurt the Yes side more than the likely-voter models assume.

I'm leaning toward No now, though the market sits near 55% Yes, which is at odds with that. I'll consider whether the market is simply thin, since it has been falling and Prop 40 failing could be pulling Prop 42 down with it.

The market quotes I'm looking at bounce between roughly 50% and 56%, and it dropped about 10 points in a day, so I'm not sure it's a reliable signal. My own estimate sits around 49–50%, which makes this close to a coin flip, and I still have to pick a side.

I'm considering how the opposition's coordinated "Yes on 40, No on 41 and 42" message might be easier for voters to follow than the separate ads from the No on 40 side, which don't mention 42. That could leave some voters who oppose 40 uncertain about 42, and possibly pushing a few toward No out of general skepticism.

I'm now weighing Prop 42 against its sibling measures: Prop 41 is trailing badly in both polls, while Prop 43, a classic anti-tax measure, is also behind, which suggests voters aren't reflexively opposed to taxes here.

I'm looking at whether the official ballot label, which says the measure nullifies post-2026 taxes that conflict with it, would read as aimed at Prop 40, and whether voters would notice that. I'm also wondering if "no one is taxing your 401(k)" would persuade Democrats, even though the retirement-protection framing polls well. Then I'm pulling up a 2024 Washington measure backed by one billionaire, though I don't think it's a close analogue.

I'm weighing whether the progressive voices publicly breaking with Newsom on 42 could move Democrats toward No, and whether the party's slate mailers telling voters to vote Yes on 40 and No on 41 and 42 would push the same way. I'm also starting to consider the other side of that question.

I'm weighing whether Prop 42 can pick up enough crossover support to pass. Its roughly 32% Democratic backing is in the range of past measures that did pass, though well short of the strongest ones.

I'm settling on a Dem support figure of about 30% as the threshold for Prop 42 to pass, and the IGS split is unclear, though Democratic Yes is probably around 25%. Weighing the trend and late voter mix, I still see this as close to a coin flip with a slight lean to No, while the market leans Yes. I'm thinking about searching for newer polling or early-ballot analysis to settle it.

I'm checking whether a Paul Mitchell analysis of Prop 42 exists.

Greed is on the California ballot, and it appears to be winning.
For a while, Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax initiative, which is supported by the state Democratic Party but opposed by many unions and prominent Democrats, was polling well. The notion of taxing the excessive wealth of the super-rich, or the basis of that wealth—the “paper profits” on a sea of unsold investments—has become increasingly popular across the nation. Nobody much likes taxation, but the way the economic spoils are distributed just isn’t working out well for most Americans, whose costs of living are growing faster than their wages, even as the wealth of the 0.00001 percent goes completely haywire (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/why-billionaires-pay-less-taxes-zucman-saez-jeff-bezos-irs-breaks-income-wealth/).
Add to that the specter of a wealthy, hyper-transactional president openly using his office (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/corruption-midterms-data-centers-epstein-stock-trading-pharma-texas-hinojosa-ossoff-sand/) to enrich himself, and his family and friends, often at taxpayer expense. The public, too, is finally starting to grasp the full extent to which our billionaires, most notably Elon Musk, are using their largely untaxed and godlike fortunes (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/04/us-federal-tax-system-progressive-oligarchy-rich-capital-unrealized-gains-wealth-inheritance-dynasty/) for political gain: dictating our ballot choices, messing with elections (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/elon-musk-is-the-midterms-biggest-disinformation-risk/), harming the nation (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/08/gao-report-doge-elon-musk-overstated-savings-wall-receipts-waste-fraud-cost/), and dodging accountability (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/oligarchy-tax-evasion-avoidance-irs-powerless-enforcement-books-blind-spot-excerpt-jeffrey-winters/).
If Prop. 40 passes, it would be the first-ever tax on excessive wealth, as opposed to income, in the United States. It would place a one-time, 5 percent levy on the net assets of California residents in excess of $1 billion. The measure, put forth by a health workers union to plug holes in the state Medicaid and education budgets created by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, immediately raised the hackles of California’s three-comma club, whose members tend to be allergic to taxation.
The claim that losing 250 billionaires would kill the state tax base and stifle innovation is laughable. They pay minimal taxes, and there are tens of thousands of Californians worth $30 million and up.
These moguls, led by Google co-founder Sergey Brin (who now claims residence in Nevada), started a group called Building a Better California (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/), which they’ve bankrolled to the tune of $333 million—about 0.1 percent of the combined net worth of its top 5 backers (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html): Brin, Google’s Steve Schmidt, venture capitalist John Doerr, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, and investor Vinod Khosla. The group has blanketed the state political landscape with anti-Prop 40 advertising and propaganda. It also bankrolled two poison pill initiatives, Props. 41 and 42, that we’ll talk about in a minute.
There are legitimate critiques of Prop. 40: Voter initiatives are a lousy way to do tax policy. Maybe it won’t bring in as much cash as projected. It’ll be challenged in court. (What isn’t?) Voters might conflate it with another measure, Prop. 3, that would extend an existing tax on income in excess of $371,000 ($742,000 for joint filers) to fund public education.
One big (valid) gripe about Prop. 40 is that it’s one-and-done. The California Teachers Union, for instance, says it opposes the measure on the grounds that it “will not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve.” Such arguments are politically safe for Democratic politicians such as Xavier Becerra—who will almost certainly replace Gavin Newsom as governor, and who opposes Prop. 40 (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/2026/07/31/becerra-announces-positions-on-key-november-ballot-measures/) (though, in true weasel fashion, he has declined to take a position on the competing propositions, 41 and 42). The fact that most of the Prop. 40 revenues are earmarked for health care also may have miffed some of the other unions that oppose it (https://www.wsj.com/politics/california-billionaire-tax-democratic-party-f4729c1d?st=99MAWA&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink), and that would prefer some of the money go toward their own interests.
But the billionaires have been hawking other, dubious concerns, which Democratic foes of Prop. 40, including Newsom, have parroted without a lot of scrutiny. For instance, the claim that Prop. 40 will end up costing California money because billionaires will flee the state, and that this would be terrible for its economy.
Former US Rep. Katie Porter, who lost her recent bid for governor, posted a video (https://www.facebook.com/katieporterca/videos/ive-spent-my-career-arguing-that-we-should-demand-bold-change-that-improves-fami/2321734451928570/) of her top three reasons to vote against Prop. 40. To paraphrase: It doesn’t accomplish any of the big things Democrats have always longed for, such as Medicare for All; It’s “big bucks for Big Insurance;” and “It’s a one-time tax that would create long-term harms” by driving “hundreds of billions in potential tax revenues out of California.”
Her first reason is clearly ridiculous. The second is misleading: State legislators would sort out the details but, per the legislative analyst, 90 percent of the tax revenue would have to be spent on “health care services for the public.” To the extent this would “line the pockets of health-care executives,” as Porter put it, well, that’s a function of America’s dysfunctional health care system (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2024/12/toll-health-insurance-industry-profits-claim-denials-delays-care-brian-thompson-unitedhealth-luigi-mangione-physicians-national-health-program/), which Prop. 40 wasn’t designed to fix. But the alternative, proponents say, is to leave millions of low-income Californians, including many children, without health insurance, and put tens of thousands of health care providers out of work.
Her third talking point is echoed by other opponents, including Newsom, who has close ties to the Getty clan and is likely running for president, which means he needs billionaires in his corner. This one is straight from the No on 40 playbook: the notion that if the measure passes, these captains of industry will pull up stakes and depart for other jurisdictions, crippling the tax base and stifling California’s engine of innovation. Early on, a handful of billionaires announced their intention to leave. “The departure of these individuals alone,” the No on 40 campaign asserted, “is estimated to remove $536 billion, or nearly 30 percent of aggregate billionaire wealth, from the tax base.” This claim, though, is based on an analysis (https://www.hoover.org/press/californias-proposed-billionaire-tax-will-cost-state-estimated-25-billion-hoover-study-finds) by the conservative Hoover Institution that prompted a detailed rebuttal from the economists who helped write Prop. 40, arguing that the Hoover study is deeply flawed (https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c15504/c15504.pdf).
There are other, more basic problems with the notion that significant wealth flight will occur and that it will harm California and stifle innovation. As I’ve written elsewhere (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/), the choice of whether to stay or go also depends on many factors unrelated to taxation, and nobody can accurately predict how most billionaires would react if Prop. 40 passed. The people making such predictions either have an agenda or are “delusional,” the former chief economist for California’s tax authority told me.
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, an outlier, has made clear he’ll stay put, and says he has no problem paying whatever taxes the state may impose. It’s a “privilege,” he told CBS News.
“I’m not afraid of paying taxes. I’m just afraid of being poor,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told @jolingkent (https://x.com/jolingkent?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw), as he explained why it would be a “privilege” to pay some $8 billion in taxes under California’s Proposition 40 – a one-time, 5% state tax on the net worth of California's… pic.twitter.com/SR3amOK1Om (https://t.co/SR3amOK1Om)
- CBS Sunday Morning 🌞 (@CBSSunday) October 19, 2026 (https://x.com/CBSSunday/status/2112234190284435529?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)
Of course, most of these tech billionaires weren’t wealthy when they started out—Huang once worked as a dishwasher (https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/magazines/panache/one-decision-that-made-jensen-huang-worth-185-billion-nvidia-nearly-went-bankrupt-in-1996-then-a-risky-bet-helped-build-its-ai-dominance/articleshow/135016538.cms?from=mdr) at Denny’s. New scrappy founders will come around and start ventures with or without the help of their predecessors. And even if all of California’s billionaires (Forbes counts 255 (https://www.forbes.com/lists/richest-in-each-state/)) were to leave and quit investing in new Silicon Valley companies, there’d still be tons of money available. The data firm Altrata, which tracks global wealth trends, estimates there are well over 22,000 ultra-high net worth individuals—people with net assets of $30 million and up—in San Francisco and Los Angeles alone. And investment, of course, can come from anywhere.
Rep. Ro Khanna doesn’t buy the claim that billionaires would flee over a 5 percent wealth tax: “They know that that is total propaganda.”
Finally, billionaire wealth is not a significant part of California’s tax base. In op-eds opposing Prop. 40, writers have pointed to the tax contributions of the state’s richest 1 percent—Newsom has even cited the top 10 percent . But billionaires comprise another realm entirely, and they already, by and large, have gone out of their way (https://www.propublica.org/article/the-secret-irs-files-trove-of-never-before-seen-records-reveal-how-the-wealthiest-avoid-income-tax) to ensure that only the tiniest sliver of their true economic income, and that of their companies, is subject to tax. Take Peter Thiel, one of the handful who say they’re already done with California. He famously used outrageous tactics (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) to accumulate more than $5 billion in a Roth IRA, a tax-free retirement account (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2022/02/retirement-savings-plans-favor-rich-wealth-gap-tax-incentives-portman-cardin-congress-secure-act/) designed for middle-class earners.
Newsom and others claim that, because billionaire wealth is portable, any wealth tax should be imposed at the federal level, not the state level, but as I made abundantly clear in my earlier piece, “How to Tax a Billionaire (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/),” a federal wealth tax is never going to fly. Not, at least, without radical changes in the Supreme Court.
Besides, billionaires have done tremendously well in California, whose tech industry was built on a foundation (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2013/10/timeline-technology-silicon-valley-government-subsidies/) of publicly funded innovation. According to Forbes , Mark Zuckerberg’s net assets grew from $64.4 billion in 2023 to $214.6 billion on Thursday—an untaxed 233 percent gain in less than three years. If you’d put $1 in the S&P 500 in September 2023, and reinvested the dividends, it would have been worth about $1.80 in September 2026.
Would billionaires really turn tail over a paltry 5 percent tax?
At a recent event in San Francisco, I posed that question to Silicon Valley congressman Ro Khanna, whose support for Prop. 40 has made him persona non grata, he told me, among the tech billionaires in his district. “They know that that is total propaganda,” Khanna replied. “The AI revolution is happening in the Bay Area—it’s not happening in Miami or Austin. More wealth continues to pile into Silicon Valley than people know what to do with. One-third of the nation’s wealth is in my district and the 50-mile area around it. So the idea that investment is going to leave is just counter to every point of data that we have.”
Prop. 40 may be less than ideal, but it would at least break the glass and create a precedent for taxing runaway wealth.
“The reason they don’t want to pay the tax is they don’t want to pay the tax,” he continued. “They simply believe they’re entitled to this wealth…that they have, through their own labor, earned every penny, because they somehow are better than the rest of us.”
So, sure, there are legitimate quibbles, and maybe Prop. 40 isn’t the greatest thing, but it does at least break the glass. It creates a precedent for taxing wealth, which is what the billionaires fear most. In the end, their argument mainly boils down to greed. They don’t need this money. The reality, as I learned while researching my 2021 book, Jackpot (http://www.readjackpot.com/) , is that the nation’s richest men—and they are mostly men—are engaged in an epic yacht-measuring contest, literal and figurative.
And they don’t know how to stop.
At the same event where I interviewed Khanna, I witnessed a barnburner of a speech from Erica Payne, executive director of Patriotic Millionaires, an advocacy group of wealthy Americans pushing for

[Showing characters 0 to 20000 of 33151. Call web_fetch with offset 20000 to keep reading.]

saner, more inclusive tax policies. It’s worth watching if you’ve got the time.
The billionaires’ quest to hoard wealth and fight taxes tooth and nail is, in Payne’s view, an addiction. “What happens when people start doing drugs?” she told the crowd. “The drug becomes disproportionately important. They need more of the drug to get the same high. Their emotional baseline changes and their braking system is less effective. So, the next time a billionaire says they don’t want to be taxed, you just say to yourself, that’s the addiction talking.”
This addiction to hoarding is what prompted the inclusion of the competing propositions I mentioned. Both are poison pills. Prop. 41 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), in addition to imposing audits on future tax initiatives, would nullify any state tax whose revenues are excluded (as Prop. 40 would be) from the spending limit voters passed in 1979. Because the two propositions are in conflict, the legislative analyst notes, Prop. 40 would likely be voided if both measures pass and Prop. 41 gets more yes votes.
The same goes for Prop. 42 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), which Newsom also supports. This measure subverts Prop. 40 by prohibiting retroactive taxes. (Prop. 40 would apply to anyone who was a California resident on January 1, 2026.) Prop. 42 also prohibits any future state tax on “personal property, business interests, and financial assets”—namely, wealth—“including assets in retirement and investment accounts.”
The billionaires are quite sneaky here. By calling out retirement savings, they are implying that ordinary people’s nest eggs are at risk. That’s really not true, but Newsom, shamefully, hasembraced the fearmongering (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/): “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes,” he said in a statement released by Prop. 42’s backers.
One never knows what will happen on Election Day, and polls are often unreliable, but the latest reputable ones, with days to go, are suggesting that Prop. 40 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html) and Prop. 41 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-prop-41-tax-audits-polls-2026.html?searchResultPosition=1) are likely to go down, whereas Prop. 42 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-prop-42-personal-property-tax-polls-2026.html?searchResultPosition=1) may well squeak by.
So much for California dreamin’.
Correction: This article was updated to reflect the S&P 500s’s correct three-year return on investment.

I'm weighing a few sources here: Mother Jones calls Prop 42 a likely squeak-by, prediction markets sit around 55% and On Point around 57%. My own trend read leans slightly No, which conflicts with the broader expert and market view leaning slightly Yes. Now I'm working out which signal to trust more, starting with a closer look at the historical analog.

I'm going through the PPIC October polls from 2020, 2022 and 2024 against their actual results. Across those ballot measures the final poll numbers miss the outcome by up to about five points in either direction, with no consistent bias. That suggests a 51% reading for Prop 42 could land anywhere from roughly 46 to 56, centered near 51.

I'm checking the IGS final polls against the actual results for seven measures, and the two-party shares come out about two points too high for Yes on average. The misses run both ways, though, so that bias is small compared with the spread.

Applying the IGS average shift to Prop 42's 48.9% gives about 46.7%, and a Prop 22-style swing would push it to roughly 55%. I'm also checking the PPIC two-party numbers against their results, where the misses run in both directions and a couple of the larger ones point toward Yes.

Averaging the PPIC two-party shift gives about 50.2% for Prop 42, and combining it with the IGS-adjusted 46.7% lands near 48.5%, which tilts No. Now I'm checking what happens if Prop 42 follows a Prop 22-style pattern, with heavy Yes spending against weak opposition.

Checking the Prop 22 case more closely, the IGS October numbers show Yes and No both gaining among undecideds, which makes me doubt that a clean analog holds. Weighting a typical measure at about 65% and a Prop 22-style result at about 35% still lands near a coin flip, around 50%.

Prop 42 has no momentum like Prop 22 did, since the Yes side's support stayed flat while No gained across both the IGS and PPIC polls. That negative trend pushes me toward treating it as a typical measure, which leans No at around 48.5%.

I'm checking whether the poll dates might have favored Yes, and whether the electorate is older than the likely-voter models assume. I also don't know what the On Point 54.2% prior is built on. Looking at the final days, the No side got a boost from the IGS coverage and the Politico "poison pill" story, along with progressive influencers and party slate cards.

I'm now looking at turnout by group: Latino voters lean strongly against Prop 42 in the PPIC poll, and if their turnout is surging, that cuts against the measure. Young voters are also heavily opposed, so elevated youth turnout would hurt it too. Independents, who lean for it, appear to be turning out at a lower rate than the other groups.

I'm running the electorate numbers: with the within-party figures, Yes comes out near 51%, and with the trend-adjusted figures closer to 49%. Either way it lands around 49–51%, so it's essentially a coin flip, and I need to settle on a side.

I'm going over the rule of thumb that measures polling around 50% in the final week usually fail, backed by DiCamillo's warning and Politico's note that campaigns want to see the low-to-mid 50s. Prop 42 sits at 51% in PPIC and 43% in IGS, which puts it below that comfort threshold.

I'm now comparing the prediction market's view with the poll-based read. The market swung from about 76% down to the low-to-mid 50s after the IGS poll came out, which suggests it reacts to headlines more than to the underlying numbers. I'm also wondering whether thin markets on obscure measures like this one are just overweighting the PPIC headline figure.

I'm now weighing whether the Newsom endorsement and the Dem slate card, which says No on 42, will cancel each other out among Democratic voters. Those cues pull in opposite directions, and I can't tell which one carries more weight with the voters who are still deciding.

I'm wondering whether Newsom's endorsement of Yes on 42 might win over Democrats who oppose Prop 40, since they overlap a lot. If opposition to Prop 40 keeps growing among Democrats, Yes on 42 could gain ground too, which cuts against my lean toward No.

Prop 42 and Prop 40 both lost Democratic support between September and October, and both lost independents too. That looks less like a split between the two measures and more like voters becoming skeptical of ballot measures generally, with Republicans holding firm on both.

I'm leaning toward No at about 52–55%, but the prediction market puts Yes at 55%, which is a real disagreement I haven't resolved. I want to check whether any other late public polls on Prop 42 exist, such as the Emerson or USC/CSU surveys, before settling.
