California 2026 Poll: Xavier Becerra Holds 27-Point Lead over Steve Hilton
October 21st, 2026
Home (https://emersoncollegepolling.com/) Polls (https://emersoncollegepolling.com/blog/) California 2026 Poll: Xavier Becerra Holds 27-Point Lead over Steve Hilton
Gov. Newsom Holds 46% Approval, 43% Disapproval Rating
A new Emerson College Polling survey of California voters finds Democrat Xavier Becerra with a 27-point lead over Republican Steve Hilton, 60% to 33%. Seven percent are undecided. After undecided voters are asked which candidate they lean toward, Becerra leads 64% to 36%.
“After receiving the plurality of votes in the open primary for Governor with 28% in June, Becerra leads Hilton in the race for Governor, outside the survey’s margin of error,” Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, said. “California independents break for Becerra by 10 points, 46% to 36%, a group Hilton would need more support among to compete in the general election.”
The economy is the top issue for 45% of California voters, along with housing affordability (17%), healthcare (10%), and immigration (10%).
When asked who they think is responsible for the current state of the California economy, 44% say President Trump, 38% Governor Newsom, 7% the Republican majority in Congress, and 8% someone else.
Compared to a year ago (https://emersoncollegepolling.com/california-2026-new-poll/), the percentage of voters who blame President Trump for the state of the California economy increased 17 points, from 27% to 44%, while those who blame Newsom decreased 13 points, from 51% to 38%.
President Trump holds a 33% approval rating; 63% disapprove of the job Trump is doing in office. Governor Gavin Newsom holds a 46% job approval rating, and 43% disapproval. Twelve percent are neutral.
Methodology
The Emerson College Polling California survey was conducted October 17-19, 2026. The overall sample of California likely voters, n=1,000, has a credibility interval, similar to a poll’s margin of error (MOE), of +/- 3.1 percent. The data sets were weighted by gender, education, party registration, and region based on U.S. Census parameters and voter file data.
It is important to remember that subsets based on demographics, such as gender, age, education, and race/ethnicity, carry with them higher credibility intervals, as the sample size is reduced. Survey results should be understood within the poll’s range of scores, and with a confidence interval of 95% a poll will fall outside the range of scores 1 in 20 times.
Data was collected by contacting registered voters from a voter file provided by Aristotle using MMS text-to-web, probability-based panel of voters provided by Consensus Strategies using MMS text-to-web, additional panel interviews were provided by PureSpectrum. All respondents were recruited using customized links that prevent responses from anyone outside of the poll’s sample frame. Panel responses were matched to the Aristotle voter file using respondents’ full name and ZIP code. The survey was administered using QuestionPro.
All questions asked in this survey with exact wording and order, along with full results, demographics, and cross tabulations can be found below.
FULL RESULTS (https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1CNKS1vdy2zMV1hVgXjxspGwEnQV0Fro_/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=107857247170786005927&rtpof=true&sd=true)

New CA Poll: Voter ID Measure Leads Today. Its Undecided Voters Point the Other Way

SAN FRANCISCO – Most polls answer one question: if the election were held today, who would win? We asked a slightly different question: who are the undecided voters, and how will they vote?
Surveys like the one sponsored by the Public Policy Institute of California are built to measure where a race stands at a particular point in time. They do that job well, in part by asking nearly every respondent to pick a side. The Independent Voter Project survey is built to study the voters who have not picked a side, or who can still be persuaded. It reports them separately, then looks at who they are.
That matters because undecided voters are not a random slice of the electorate. Who is still undecided varies by each race and ballot question, and the makeup of that group best guides where a close contest is likely to land.
For example, Proposition 39, the voter ID measure, leads in our survey, 43 percent to 40 percent among likely voters, with 17 percent undecided. But the Republicans we surveyed have largely made up their minds, and the voters who haven't are mostly Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents. If those voters break the way similar voters already have, Prop. 39 lands at about 50 percent, a coin flip, but if they follow the usual pattern of voters who are unsure about a ballot measure and vote no, it will fail.
The survey of 2,906 likely voters was conducted Sept. 23 to Oct. 2, 2026 in English and Spanish and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Details are in the methodology section at the end of this story. Six weeks before the June 2 primary, an IVP poll (https://ivn.us/tag/ivp-poll/)was the first published survey in the New York Times tracker (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-governor-election-polls-2026.html?ref=ivn.us) to show Xavier Becerra breaking away (https://ivn.us/breaking-xavier-becerra-bolts-into-first-place-in-ivn-california-governor-poll-2026-04-20/) from the Democratic field for governor. He finished first.
Where the contests stand among likely voters today; undecided voters are shown in gold. How the Analysis Works
For each contest, the survey separates voters into those who have decided, including those who lean one way, and those who have not. It then compares undecided voters with decided ones on party, which party they trust, age, turnout history, region, and answers to related questions, such as whether they support voter ID in principle.
A statistical model trained on decided voters estimates how undecided voters with the same characteristics would likely vote. The model correctly predicts decided voters' choices about 9 times in 10 in the governor's race and on Props. 39 and 40.
The result is not a prediction of what will happen. It estimates where each contest is likely to end up if nothing changes between now and Election Day. Campaigns, news, and turnout can all change that.
Where the Contests Are Likely to Land
Likely outcomes are shares of the two-way vote if nothing changes before Election Day. Decided voters today compared with the likely outcome and range for each contest. The undecided vote looks different in every contest. On Prop. 39, it is heavily Democratic. In the insurance commissioner race, it looks much like the electorate as a whole, because so few voters know either candidate.
Who is still undecided: the makeup of the undecided vote changes from contest to contest. Prop. 39: Who Is Left to Decide
Asked the Voter ID question in plain terms, 62 percent of voters support requiring a government-issued ID to vote, with a free ID card for anyone who asks. However, the measure itself is much closer. Its official title, written by the Attorney General's office, says it "Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification."
When read this title, Republicans support Prop. 39, 81 percent to 10 percent, and only 9 percent are undecided. Democrats oppose it 59 percent to 19 percent, and more than one in five are undecided.
Of the voters still undecided on Prop. 39, 61 percent are registered Democrats, 24 percent are independents and 15 percent are Republicans. More than half of these undecided voters say they trust the Democratic Party more than the Republican Party.
To pass, Prop. 39 needs about 4 in 10 of its undecided voters, and our model estimates it gets about 41 percent. That leaves almost no cushion, and voters who are unsure about a ballot measure often vote no.
In the second wave of the survey, undecided voters were asked which way they would lean if they had to choose. Eight in 10 still could not say.
Prop. 40: Undecided Voters Don't Know Enough Yet
The idea of a one-time tax on billionaires to fund health care splits voters 40 percent to 38 percent. Prop. 40 itself trails 38 percent to 42 percent after voters hear the Legislative Analyst's Office estimate that it would raise tens of billions of dollars but could cost up to $1 billion a year in income tax revenue if wealthy residents leave California.
Its undecided voters are a different group. They are about half Democrats, a quarter independents, and a quarter Republicans. Most of them are not sure about the idea of a wealth tax at all: 62 percent of Prop. 40's undecided voters were also still undecided when the tax was described in plain terms .
To pass, Prop. 40 would need about 6 in 10 of its undecided voters. The model estimates it gets about half. In this survey, that makes Prop. 40 a toss-up that leans toward "No." PPIC's September survey found Prop. 40 ahead, and the difference between the two polls comes largely from Democratic and Latino voters, who are more supportive of the measure in PPIC's survey than in the one conducted by IVP.
Prop. 41, which would require audits of new special taxes, and Prop. 42, which would block new taxes on the ownership of financial assets and personal property, both lead comfortably. Our questions described those measures in plain terms rather than using their ballot labels, so read the size of their leads with caution. Because Props. 40, 41 and 42 conflict, the one with the most yes votes takes effect.
Support for Props. 39 to 42 by party registration. Insurance Commissioner: Two Democrats, and Most Voters Have No Idea
The race for Insurance Commissioner between state Sen. Ben Allen and Jane Kim, both Democrats, is the most open contest on California's ballot this November.
In the IVP survey, half of respondents saw only the candidates' names, as they will see them on the ballot. When given this choice, nearly two-thirds had no opinion, and the horse race was within the margin of error.
The other half of the IVP survey respondents were told that the Democratic Socialists of America endorse Jane Kim and that Ben Allen is a mainstream Democrat. With that one bit of information, Allen leads Kim, 36 percent to 23 percent, and his likely share of the two-way vote rises to about 63 percent. Republicans and independents supply most of the movement toward Allen, while Democrats stayed nearly evenly divided.
The insurance commissioner’s race will turn on what voters learn about the differences between the two Democrats on the ballot and whether Republicans, who have no candidate of their own, actually fill in the line and vote for one of the Democrats. Shown only names, nearly one in four Republicans said they would skip voting in this race.
The Los Angeles mayor's race features the same kind of matchup in a city with far fewer Republican voters. A recent UC Berkeley poll (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/politics/nithya-raman-karen-bass-la-mayor-election-polls/3946109/?ref=ivn.us) shows the DSA-endorsed challenger, City Councilmember Nithya Raman, leading Mayor Karen Bass, with a third of voters undecided.
Half of the respondents saw only names. Half were told that DSA endorses Kim and that Allen is a mainstream Democrat. Governor and the Down-Ballot Races
Xavier Becerra leads Steve Hilton 48 percent to 38 percent. Fifty-five percent of the undecided voters in our survey are Democrats, and the model estimates they will break about 2-to-1 Becerra’s way. Hilton would need about 9 in 10 undecided voters to win. If nothing changes, Becerra's likely share of the two-way vote is about 57 percent.
The races for lieutenant governor and secretary of state have even more undecided voters, about one in four, and the undecideds are the same makeup as in the race for governor. Democrats Fiona Ma and Shirley Weber are likely to win their elections with 57 and 59 percent, respectively, if nothing changes. Republicans Gloria Romero and Don Wagner would each need about 7 in 10 undecided voters to break in their favor to win.
Independents Are the Swing Within the Swing
Independent voters, those registered with No Party Preference, the American Independent Party, or another minor party, make up about a quarter of likely California voters. They make up a larger share of the undecided vote, close to a third, in the races for lieutenant governor and secretary of state.
Independents are not one bloc. More lean toward Democrats than Republicans: 29 percent trust the Democratic Party more, compared with 24 percent who trust the Republican Party more, and each group votes much like the party it trusts.
The largest group, though, 40 percent of independent voters, trusts neither party, even when asked to choose.
Those voters are where the close contests are most open:
They lean slightly toward Hilton, 40 percent to 33 percent, with nearly one in five undecided.
They support Prop. 39, 49 percent to 32 percent. That is the one group outside the Republican base where the measure has real support.
They split on Prop. 40, 36 percent to 40 percent, with nearly a quarter undecided.
Nearly half are undecided in the insurance commissioner race even after hearing which candidate DSA endorses.
Taken together, independents split about evenly in the governor's race.
They are also the voters most likely to leave part of the ballot blank. Only 65 percent of independents say they will vote on every race and measure, compared with 78 percent of Democrats and 75 percent of Republicans.
Which Independents Are Still Undecided
The independents who remain undecided are not the same voters from one contest to the next. The survey asked every respondent which party they trust more if they had to choose, and the answer changes the picture race by race.
Undecided independents by the party they trust more, if they had to choose. Governor. Republican-leaning independents have almost all decided. Only 3 percent of undecided independents in the governor's race trust Republicans more. Seven in 10 trust neither party. Independents who have already made up their minds split almost evenly between Becerra and Hilton, but undecided independents are likely to break about 63 percent for Becerra. Hilton's independents are already counted. The remaining voters are not his natural base.
Secretary of State. Only 1 in 10 undecided independents trusts Republicans more, and they are likely to break about 63 percent for Weber, compared with 53 percent among decided independents. The lieutenant governor's race is the exception among the candidate races: its undecided independents split about evenly, just as the decided ones do.
Prop. 39. Only 15 percent of Prop. 39's undecided independents trust Republicans more than Democrats. (Overall, 25 percent of independents trust Republicans.) The rest of the undecideds lean Democratic or trust neither party. Independents who have already made up their minds support the measure 58 percent to 42 percent. Undecided independents are likely to split about evenly. More than 4 in 10 of them are not sure about voter ID even in principle.
Prop. 40. Undecided independents on this question lean Democratic, which makes them more likely to vote yes than the independents who have already made up their minds. In other words, the conservative-leaning independent voters have already taken a side.
Insurance commissioner. With only names to go on, the undecided independents look like independents as a whole, including Republican-leaning voters. Almost no one knows the candidates, so party trust has not sorted anyone yet. That is why the race moves so sharply once voters learn who DSA endorses.
Undecided independents are likely to break differently than independents who have already decided. The groups of undecided independents are small, from about 80 to 230 respondents depending on the contest, so these figures show direction more than precise size.

content.thinking:
I've got the polls in hand now, and they don't settle Prop 42 on their own. The final numbers put Yes slightly ahead in some and No slightly ahead in another, so I'm weighing the averages and the undecided share. I'm now turning to the trend across the polling period.

Now I'm weighing the rest of the evidence: the money, endorsements, and turnout all lean toward No, while the market and model lean toward Yes.

I'm testing whether the Prop 40 result could carry Prop 42 along with it, since the two would tend to move together. Using the market and PPIC figures, I'm estimating that Prop 42 lands around 50-51% if Prop 40 goes down with its expected leakage.

Prop 40's likely final result is what decides Prop 42 here: if it lands around 54% No, Prop 42 probably passes at 51-53%, but a 52% No leaves it a toss-up. I'm weighing whether Prop 40's sharp decline reflects broad "No on everything" sentiment, which would also drag on Prop 42, or a targeted rejection of the wealth tax.

I'm checking how Prop 40's shifting support lines up with Prop 42: from September to October, Prop 40's No rose while Prop 42's Yes fell, so the new opponents of 40 weren't simply moving over to 42. Earlier there was an overlap of voters backing both, and by October that overlap seems to have disappeared.

I'm trying to work out whether the Yes-on-both voters split toward No on 40 or No on 42, since Prop 40 Yes dropped about six points while Prop 42 Yes dropped about three. If the sorting finishes cleanly, Prop 42 Yes should land near Prop 40 No minus whoever is opposed to both.

I'm working through how the Prop 40 and Prop 42 voters overlap: the "No on both" group is what would pull Prop 42's Yes share below Prop 40's No share, so I'm trying to estimate how big that group is and whether it grows as the measures get sorted out.

I'm estimating Prop 40's final margin next: the market puts its passage at about 21%, and the polls average near 47-48% Yes, which I'd nudge down a couple of points for late movement and heavy No spending, landing around 46%. That in turn sets where Prop 42 ends up.

I'm working out Prop 40's likely final margin at about 45-46% Yes, which puts Prop 42 near 51-52% if it tracks closely. That still leaves some uncertainty, and my rough chance of Prop 42 clearing 50% is around 64%. The gap between the two measures in the IGS poll looks wider, so I'm checking whether the tracking assumption holds.

I'm finding Prop 42 at about 51% if Prop 40's No share is around 54.5% and the usual gap of roughly 3 points holds. That gives a modest Yes lean, which matches the market and the model. But my earlier calibration with the typical pollster bias gave about 48.5%, so I need to check which shift I should be applying.

I'm weighing whether late deciders are "No on everything" voters, who would drag Prop 42 down along with Prop 40, or anti-wealth-tax voters, who would only move Prop 40. The two readings give very different answers, so I'm checking the IGS shifts to see which dominates.

Looking at the IGS and PPIC shifts from September to October, both No shares climbed together: Prop 40 No went up by 8 and 6 points, and Prop 42 No by 11 and 4. That pattern points to late deciders rejecting both measures rather than splitting between them. If that carries through, Prop 42's remaining undecided voters would likely break No and pull it toward 45-47%.

I'm now questioning the "No on everything" reading: if it held, Prop 42 would sit below the PPIC figure of 51%, closer to 47-49%. Democrats seem to be turning No on both measures, since Prop 40 Yes is falling rather than rising as it would under party-slate voting.

The newspaper endorsements matter here, since several major papers recommended No on 40, 41, and 42, which gives moderate Democrats a ready-made "No on all three" slate to follow. That would explain why No is rising on both measures rather than splitting between them.

I'm working out what the "No on both" group could mean for Prop 42: if it's around 6-8% and the "Yes on both" group shrinks to 2-3%, Prop 42 would land near 49-51% against Prop 40's No share of 54-55%. That's still too close to call, so I'm weighing how measures near 50% in late polls usually fare.

I'm recalling how similar measures near 50% in recent California elections turned out: Prop 32 in 2024 polled close and failed narrowly, while Prop 34 passed by a hair, so near-50% polling doesn't reliably predict either outcome.

I'm running through past California measures polling near 50% and how they actually turned out. Some failed narrowly, some passed narrowly, so a close poll doesn't clearly point either way. A few 2018 and 2020 measures that were close in the polls split just as unpredictably.

I'm weighing whether the 2020 Prop 19 polling is worth recalling here, though I'm not confident about how it ended up. The opposition to Prop 42 comes from the Democratic Party, parts of labor, progressive leaders, and many newspapers, while its backers include Newsom, the most visible Democrat in the state. I'm comparing that coalition against earlier measures that drew heavy spending and still squeaked past.

I'm weighing the coalition behind Prop 42: firefighters and building trades on one side, with police, and teachers as messengers. Their ad spending is a powerful combination, and it's a sharp contrast to Prop 22's drivers. Older voters, who turn out most reliably, back the measure strongly in the PPIC data, so I'm checking how that age split translates into a final share.

Breaking the age split down further, the 55+ group, which turns out most reliably, drives most of the Yes share. Depending on whether the youth share lands near 18% or 22%, the estimate stays around 50-51%, so I'll go with roughly 51% for now.

I'm weighing the market and model consensus, which leans Yes at around 55-57%, against the trend-based read that leans No. The money also favors Yes, and while the rule of thumb that a measure below 50% and falling tends to fail fits the IGS numbers, PPIC still has it at 51%, so I'm checking which pollster has been more reliable this cycle.

I'm comparing how the IGS and PPIC polls each handled earlier measures: PPIC's Prop 32 read too negative in 2024, while IGS's two-party figure ran too positive, and in 2020 both overstated the Yes side on Prop 15.

I'm checking the two pollsters' track records on this kind of measure: across Props 32, 15, 22, and 16, averaging the PPIC and IGS two-party shares lands about half a point too high on average, with the misses ranging from roughly 5 points too positive to 3.6 too negative.

I'm turning the averaged two-party figure for Prop 42, about 50.5%, into a rough chance of passing: with a spread of around 3.5 points, that comes to roughly 55%, which lines up with the market. A negative trend would pull that down by half a point or so, and the heavy Yes spending would push it back up, so I'm treating this as close to a coin flip.

I'm weighing the case for Yes: the campaign against Prop 40 is going well, which could carry over to Prop 42, Newsom's backing gives moderate Democrats cover, and the firefighter messengers and "protect retirement" framing, plus the $157M, all work in its favor. Against that, the Democratic slate opposes it, polling momentum is negative, and voter fatigue with so many measures tends to default toward No.

I'm going back over the Prop 3 voters, since most of them are likely Democrats who would vote No on 42, and I'm estimating how many Prop 3 No voters would have to cross over to make up the gap. Then I'm turning to the 2026 partisan lean, where Becerra's margin is the key figure.

I'm checking what share of Becerra's voters would have to back Prop 42 to reach 50%: if Hilton's voters split 88% Yes, Becerra's side needs roughly 28% Yes, which is about what PPIC shows among Democrats, so it sits right at the threshold. IGS likely has a similar Becerra lead and puts Prop 42 at 43-45%.

I'm still torn on whether Prop 42 passes, since the market and models put it near 55% while my own read sits closer to 50%. I'm weighing whether the Kalshi price, which fell from about 76% to 55% after the October polls, reflects real information or just a bias toward the big-money side.

I'm checking whether the pollsters' record matters here, and I'm weighing Newsom's track record of backing measures that pass, even though he's at odds with his own party on this one.

I'm checking whether Newsom has been personally campaigning for Prop 42 or just lending his name to it, since so far he seems to have only endorsed it, while putting his energy into opposing Prop 40. I'm also thinking about the Kalshi market on whether Prop 42 gets more Yes votes than Prop 40, which sits around 63-70%, and how that comparison might play out if Prop 42 lands near 48%.

I'm wondering whether the No on 40 campaign, which the same donors funded, is urging voters to also vote Yes on 42, since that cross-promotion could matter a lot. I'm not sure whether their mailers actually say that, and the coalition behind them, including CTA, may shape how that messaging lands.

I'm weighing whether the Democrats who back the No on 40 campaign will also vote Yes on 42, since the cues are mixed: Newsom supports it, the party opposes it, and Becerra and CTA have stayed neutral. I suspect a meaningful share of moderate Democrats will land on No on both, which would explain the gap IGS shows.

I'm now judging the median voter: a moderate Democrat or Dem-leaning independent who likely votes No on 40 and Yes on 3, and who sees both Newsom's endorsement and the party's and newspapers' opposition to 42. That mix makes me think this voter is roughly indifferent, so I'm settling on a estimate just under even odds with a slight lean toward failing.

I'm breaking the PPIC results down by ideology and region: moderates lean Yes 53-44, liberals strongly No, conservatives strongly Yes, and a weighted mix of those comes out around 52%. Regionally, the Bay Area and LA are close to even against it, while Orange/San Diego, the Inland Empire, and the Central Valley lean Yes, leaving the statewide figure at 51%.

I'm comparing PPIC's record on measures near 51% with heavy Yes-side spending. Earlier ones like Prop 22 finished above their PPIC numbers, but Prop 1 in 2024 fell far short of its poll, though that was a low-turnout primary.

I'm considering whether PPIC's likely voter screen skews toward older, habitual voters, which could overstate Yes support if this election draws in more young and Latino first-time voters who lean No on Prop 42.

I'm adjusting the Prop 42 estimate down about a point, since surging turnout among young and Latino voters, who oppose it by wide margins, could mean PPIC's likely-voter sample overstates Yes support. That puts me near 49.5%, which leaves me leaning slightly toward No, though I want to recheck that against the market's read.

I'm settling on On Point's forecast landing near 49.7% once the early-ballot electorate is accounted for, and I'm setting aside roll-off, since skippers are mostly low-information and matter little. I'm also considering whether some voters might back the measure privately, out of concern for their own savings, even in a Democratic-leaning state.

I'm weighing whether the market's 55% Yes and the experts' "could go either way" framing point the same direction. The Mother Jones writer, who opposes the measure, still expects it may squeak by, and Politico noted that a PPIC poll showing it passing is not the likeliest outcome.

I'm weighing whether Brin's group, having spent heavily in October and kept pushing Prop 42 after abandoning Prop 41, saw favorable internal numbers that made the measure look winnable. Continued spending of that size suggests they regard it as close but within reach, or that they're buying insurance in case Prop 40 passes and Prop 42 has to carry the day.

I'm settling on roughly even odds for Prop 42, leaning on the idea that its "protect your retirement savings" pitch could appeal to voters who are opposing Prop 40 and see the two as a pair. I'm treating the No on 40 ads' message about savings being taxed as a possible tailwind for Yes on 42, though I'm not sure how strong that effect really is.

I'm noting that the Citrin-POLITICO poll found most voters doubted the tax would stay limited to billionaires, and that the No on 40 side's strongest argument was that it could later reach non-billionaires. A message like "protect your retirement and savings from new taxes" would naturally appeal to that same concern, so I think it gives Prop 42 a real boost.

I'm weighing the claim that opponents of Prop 40 may still oppose Prop 42, since it bans wealth taxes outright, and the newspapers' view that it narrows options too far. The market sits at 55% Yes, On Point at 57%, and my own poll average at about 50.5%.

I'm weighing the trend now: PPIC's Yes support slid from 54 to 51 between early September and late October while No rose to 47, so the margin has been narrowing by roughly a point a week. Set against the money and the pairing with the anti-40 message, I land around 50–52% Yes, with only a very slight lean toward passing.

Running the trend through to the average ballot date, the PPIC margin shifts from about +4 to roughly +1 to +2.5 for Yes, while the IGS margin drops from −2 to about −4 to −5. That puts the two polls on different sides of even.

I'm settling the estimate near 49.5 to 50.5 percent, which reads as a true coin flip. Trends often plateau as campaigns saturate, and the early ballots were cast when Yes looked stronger. I'm also weighing the wider environment: in a Democratic-leaning year, party cues from the state party's No on 42 position may matter more, nudging toward No.

I'm weighing how a market at 51% for the measure, with the Democratic Party opposing it in a Democratic-leaning year, might read to traders who anchor on the big money and PPIC's number while discounting the IGS poll. A seasoned consultant would likely call a measure polling 51 in one survey and 43 in another, and trending down, more likely to fail than pass.

I'm checking the Republican and NPP-leaning-Republican share of the electorate, which works out to about 31% of the total for Yes, so Prop 42 would need roughly 30% of the remaining Democratic-leaning voters to clear the line. That's right at the threshold, and the momentum points toward a narrow failure, though the market and my model still lean slightly toward passage. I'm turning next to the IGS poll's already-voted subgroup for Prop 42 to see whether early ballots tell a different story.

I'm checking whether the IGS tabulations split Prop 42 support between voters who've already cast ballots and those who haven't, so I'll try a different link to the PDF.

Now I'm looking at the IGS voting breakdown for Prop 42, comparing the yes, no, and undecided shares across the four groups.

I'm checking whether the totals square with the vote splits by group: already-voted and not-yet-voted shares should weight the "total" column, and the "not a likely voter" column seems to be pulling the undecided figure up sharply.

I'm trying to make the column totals reconcile with the already-voted and not-yet-voted splits, and the weights don't come out consistently for the yes and no rows. Maybe I've got the column order wrong, so I'm checking the header labels against the four values in each row.

I'm trying to work out which four columns those values belong to, since the consistency check fails under the obvious labeling. If the first value is the total, the weighting against the already-voted and not-yet-voted shares doesn't reconcile for both the yes and no rows, so I'm questioning the column order.

Now I'm checking the Prop 42 weights against the Prop 40 benchmark, using roughly a 25/75 split between already-voted and not-yet-voted respondents, to see whether the Yes total follows the same pattern.

I'm testing whether the 25/75 already-voted and not-yet-voted weights reproduce the Yes and No totals for Prop 42, and they don't: the figures land near 44 and 43 rather than 43 and 45. The column assignments may be different from what I assumed, so I'm not treating the snippet as reliable.

I'm still trying to pin down which column each of the four Prop 42 values belongs to, since the totals don't reconcile under the obvious labeling. I'm testing whether a different assignment, maybe with a party or other subgroup in the first position, fits the numbers better, but none of the options I've tried so far work cleanly.

I'm checking the Prop 42 numbers against a 40/60 already-voted weighting, and the Yes and No totals still don't line up cleanly. The column assignments are probably what's off, so I'm not trusting the reconciliation yet.

I'm testing whether a share of about 0.42 already-voted respondents reproduces the totals, since the Yes and No figures come out close to 44 and 45 under that weighting, with the undecided row landing near 11 to 12.

I'm noticing the already-voted share implied by these numbers comes out near 42%, which clashes with the "about one-quarter" figure from the Prop 40 release, so the column labels may not mean what I assumed. Taken at face value, the already-voted group leans No on Prop 42 by about 10 points, while the not-yet-voted group leans Yes by 5 with roughly 15% undecided, which runs against what I'd expect from older, habitual early voters.

The early voters went No on both 40 and 42, which fits a habitual, older, Democratic-leaning group following the "No on 40, 41, 42" recommendations. Among the not-yet-voted, Prop 42 leads 45 to 40 with 15% undecided. If those undecideds break two-to-one No, the race ends up roughly even.

I'm weighing the IGS early-voter numbers against the SurveyUSA result, which showed early voters strongly opposed to Prop 40. I'm weighing the early-voter numbers against the overall IGS split, which puts Prop 42 at 43-45 with 12% undecided. The habitual early voters look like they're voting No on both measures, while the not-yet-voted group leans Yes, which is hard to square with what I'd expect, so I'm treating the overall result as close to a coin flip.

I'm weighing the case for Yes, which rests on PPIC's probability-based 51-47 result, a prediction market near 55%, and the large money advantage. Prop 40's failure also suggests many of those voters will back 42. On the No side, the larger and more recent IGS poll shows momentum moving against it, and both polls are trending downward.

I'm estimating the final Yes share with a simple model: averaging the probability-based PPIC result with the IGS result, then adjusting down for the late trend and the turnout mix, puts the mean just under 50%. That gives me roughly a 44% chance Yes clears 50, well below the market's 55%.

I'm weighing the trend adjustment: the Yes side kept spending heavily, the No side had little money, and the final-week coverage leaned against the measure. I'm also thinking about diminishing returns on the Yes ad spending and whether voter fatigue at Prop 42, the 12th of 14 measures, pushes people toward skipping or voting No. That leaves me leaning No at around 52-55% confidence, though the market sits at 55% for Yes.

I'm weighing the market's 55% Yes against my own estimate, and I'm recalling that Prop 32 was favored in markets before it failed. If the markets leaned too hard on the IGS lead, they may be overrating Yes on Prop 42 now.

I'm checking the PPIC 51-47 figure against the other polls, and the market's roughly 95% confidence on Prop 36 in 2024 as a reminder that markets can be right about outcomes. I still lean No, but I'm wary of overriding the market and model consensus with my own subjective adjustments. I'm settling on a lean toward No, around 55-60%. IGS has usually overestimated Yes on eroding measures, so Prop 42 finishing above its 48.9% two-party share would be unusual, unless heavy funding makes it an exception like Prop 22.

I'm running through past measures that passed with heavy spending on one side, like Props 1, 35 and 36, along with Prop 22's large yes-side lead, to see whether big money usually carries these close races. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Proposition 42 is an initiated constitutional amendment appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California. [ 1 ] California currently taxes income from financial assets but does not tax the ownership of assets such as stocks and investment accounts. [ 1 ] Proposition 42 would establish a constitutional prohibition on new state taxes on personal-property ownership, including financial assets, business interests, intellectual property and assets held in retirement accounts. [ 1 ] It would also restrict certain retroactive state taxes. [ 1 ] Even if voters approve Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), the billionaire tax, Proposition 42 could block it from taking effect if it receives more "yes" votes. [ 1 ]
Background and development
[ edit (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_42&action=edit&section=1) ]
Proposition 42 emerged during the campaign over a proposed billionaire wealth tax (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40), subsequently numbered Proposition 40 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_40). The wealth-tax initiative was backed by Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEIU_United_Healthcare_Workers_West). Its president, Dave Regan, worked with economist Emmanuel Saez and other academics on developing the proposal following federal Medicaid cuts in President Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act). # Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
***Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.*** The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

I'm weighing the evidence now, though no results are in yet, so I need to settle on a call. The two strongest polls put the race roughly even: PPIC has Yes ahead by 4, while IGS has No ahead by 2 with 12% still undecided. Both show Yes slipping over recent weeks, which is the part I want to keep in view as I weigh the rest.

I'm now weighing the spending gap, with Yes at roughly $157M and climbing against almost nothing dedicated to No, along with the partisan picture: strong Democratic turnout, the state party opposing, and Newsom in support. Prediction markets and the forecast model sit around 55 to 57 percent for Yes, and I'm checking that against the historical pattern where measures under 50 percent with eroding support usually fail. My overall estimate is still about even, and the tiebreakers point in different directions.

I'm checking whether the internal polls from the No on 40 side point the same way. If their methodology is stronger, the public polls may be overstating Prop 40 support, which would help Prop 42. I'm also weighing that Prop 42 drew a $65M commitment in October, which suggests the backers saw it as viable.

I'm now looking at Newsom's October 9 endorsement, and whether his team would have read the polling and backed a measure they expected to pass. Politicians tend to endorse likely winners, but the ideological opposition to wealth taxes may have driven it as well.

I'm checking whether the internal No on 40 polls, which put Prop 40 in the high 30s or low 40s, suggest the public polls overstate support for it. If Prop 40 is in fact lower by a few points, Prop 42 could land somewhere around 49 to 55 percent, which would be a meaningful argument for Yes.

I'm now going back to the early-voter data: SurveyUSA found 65-30 No on Prop 40 among people who'd already voted, and IGS had 53-40 against it. If early voters lean that hard against Prop 40, the final Prop 40 share could come in lower than the public polls suggest, though I still need to check how those voters split on Prop 42.

Working through the early-voter numbers, I'm estimating Prop 40 at roughly 42 to 43 percent once the early and late voters are weighted together, which would put No on Prop 40 somewhere around 55 to 57 percent.

Now I'm weighing whether early voters lean the same way on Prop 42 as they do on Prop 40, since that determines whether the early-vote shift actually helps Yes. The assumption that early No-on-40 voters also back Prop 42 looks shaky. Older, habitual voters might reject both measures, so the leakage estimate could be too generous.

I'm checking the older-voter numbers: PPIC has 55+ at 61-36 for Prop 42, and IGS has 65+ strongly against Prop 40. Since early voters skew older, early ballots probably lean toward Prop 42, while the younger late-voting groups could pull it back down.

I'm working through the early-voter math, and it lands around 50 percent. The anti-wealth-tax momentum is clearly hurting Prop 40, but Prop 42's own polling has been drifting down since September, so that momentum isn't carrying over to it.

Now I'm checking how No-on-40 voters are likely to split on Prop 42. The party crosstabs in PPIC show the two measures moving almost in lockstep, but IGS has more undecideds on 42, so the leakage estimate depends on which way they break.

I'm working out what the final Prop 40 result has to look like. If it gets crushed to around 40%, Prop 42 probably passes, but if it loses narrowly near 47%, Prop 42 probably fails. The prediction market has Prop 40 at about 21% to pass, which points to an expected Yes share of roughly 46 to 47%.

I'm running the numbers on Prop 40 now. A narrow loss would leave Prop 42 around 48 to 50 percent, but if the internal polls are right and Prop 40 falls to the low 40s, Prop 42 could reach 52 to 55. Weighing the public polls and the late shift, I'm landing on Prop 40 near 43 to 45 percent, which puts Prop 42 around 51, so I'm going with Yes.

I'm rechecking my earlier estimate: the pollsters' average, around 50.5%, has historically been roughly unbiased, which puts Yes near 55%. The downward polling trend and the spending advantage roughly offset each other, so I'm settling on about 53 to 55 percent for Yes. The IGS erosion signal conflicts with PPIC's numbers, and blending them still lands near 50.5%, so I'm going with yes.

content.text:
**Yes.** It's very close to a coin flip, but Yes looks slightly more likely to win. Results weren't out when I checked: AP's live page still showed 0% counted.

**For Yes:**
- **PPIC poll (Oct 16–22):** 51–47 Yes. Republicans backed it 84–15, independents 53–43, and about a third of Democrats (32%) supported it too.
- **Money:** supporters raised about $138–157M, mostly from Sergey Brin's group, with $65M put in during October alone. There was almost no money spent specifically against it; the opposing union committee's funds went mainly to Prop 40.
- **Endorsements:** Gov. Newsom, the firefighters' union, the building-trades unions, the main police union, the state Republican Party and CalChamber all back it. Its "protect your retirement savings" message plays well with older midterm voters.
- **Prop 40 is losing:** prediction markets give the billionaire tax about a 21% chance of passing. In PPIC's poll, Yes on 42 tracks No on 40 almost exactly, so a clear defeat for Prop 40 should carry 42.
- **Markets and forecasters:** Kalshi and Polymarket put Prop 42 at about 54–56% to pass. The On Point Politics forecast gives it 57%.

**For No:**
- **Berkeley IGS poll (Oct 19–25):** 43–45 No, with 12% undecided. Opposition rose 11 points since September while support stayed flat.
- **Downward trend:** PPIC also slipped, from 54% to 51%. Measures under 50% in late polls that are losing ground usually fail.
- **Opponents:** the state Democratic Party, the California Labor Federation and most Bay Area and Sacramento newspapers oppose it.
- **Turnout:** early ballots lean heavily Democratic, and young and Latino voters, who oppose it, are turning out in larger numbers than in 2022.

The prediction markets are thin, and my own estimate puts the final Yes vote around 50–52%, so a narrow loss is entirely plausible.
